# T9Sim Rebuild Plan (v2.2)

**Forked 21 August 2026 from `T9Sim_Rebuild_Plan_v2.md`. Not a schedule.** Everything below the
v2.2 scope section is v2's plan, carried over unchanged, and still governs.

**This forks from v2, NOT from v2.1.** `T9Sim_Rebuild_Plan_v2.1.md` is ABANDONED (Ken, 21 Aug 2026)
— no confidence in it. Its additions are isolated in `T9Sim_Rebuild_Plan_v2.1_ddition.md` so that
nothing is inherited silently and anything worth keeping is re-adopted deliberately.

## V2.2 scope (21 August 2026)

### Why v2.2 exists

v2 was built 11–17 August and is trusted: seven gates PASS, 77 tests green from a clean clone, and
stages 2–3 reproduce byte-identical at all three scales. Its final commit is `871d7b6`, which is now
also `main`.

The work done between 17 and 21 August is **not** trusted. It sits on three stacked branches —
`t9v2-two-bidders` contains `t9v2-arm1` contains `t9v2-persistence`, thirteen commits in all — and it
addresses real gaps, but Ken's judgement (21 Aug) is that the planning and coding degraded over that
period. v2.2 rebuilds that work properly from the trusted base rather than merging it.

### What v2.2 builds

Four workstreams. The first reimplements what already exists; the other three are new.

**1. The thirteen commits, reimplemented well.** The problems they solve are real and stay solved:

| From | What it addressed |
|---|---|
| `t9v2-persistence` | training and evaluation wrote no persistent frozen predictor as an artifact, and the recommended bid prices were neither recorded nor used in measurement and reporting. Frozen bundles, per-row eval files, calibration moved from the logged bid to the recommended bid, a ROAS gate. **Carries the artifact-retention rule** added to section 5 on 21 Aug 2026: bundles, per-row eval files and the master parquet are written and never deleted, enforced in `is_complete` rather than in prose |
| `t9v2-arm1` | the floor fix (both price shapes divide by the paying median) and the **1000× units bug** (profit reported in CPM-sums). **Both are worth keeping regardless of the branch's standing** |
| `t9v2-two-bidders` | an AFT head beside the CLF head, both bidding, reported independently across training, evaluation, inference, measurement and reporting; tilt-sweep coverage |

Arm 2 — a censoring-aware price head meant to make the two predictors cooperate — was abandoned in
August because the design never settled how they relate. v2.2 keeps them **independent**, which was
the two-bidders position and is the one that worked.

**2. A price feature that lets more SSP information reach C3.** Added to the schema and the node
register, with a new design fingerprint, which invalidates all 30 existing datasets. The design
belongs in the Specification, not here; the open definitions are listed below.

**3. Survival regression → plain regression.** Enabled by workstream 2. If the target becomes
observable rather than interval-censored, the AFT machinery is no longer required. Whether this is a
clean switch or a partial one depends on the row-visibility decision below.

**4. An oracle ceiling for the win head.** Every headline metric is scored against an oracle except
the win head, so the SSP contrast — the study's central claim — is the one number with no reference
point. Raised 13 July 2026 ("Tier-2 Bayes ceiling: NOT run") and independently again in August; never
closed. `oracle_bidder_ev` already computes the true win curve, so this is scoring-side work with no
regeneration. Cheapest of the four.

### The build order (agreed 22 August 2026)

**The method, settled 21–22 August.** Design on paper first, then build in dependency-ordered steps
with a review after each, batch the single regeneration, and produce every number of record from one
campaign at the end. Neither extreme was taken: not feature-by-feature with a full rebuild each time,
which pays for the campaign twice and builds the price head against censored data before the
regression decision deletes it; and not plan-everything-then-build-in-one-go, which lands roughly
2,700 lines of source unreviewed and cannot localise a gate failure.

**Gates run by blast radius, not seven per feature.** Seven gates per feature would mean eight campaigns; no gates until the end is how the 17–21 August work went wrong. One complete seven-gate pass at the end is the release check.

**Which gates a step runs is decided by REVIEW, not by a lookup table (Ken, 22 August 2026).** A fixed mapping was drafted and rejected: it goes stale, and the case it would miss is the one that matters — a step touching an artifact nobody predicted. So at the end of every step, walk all seven gates and record the verdict on each:

> | Gate | Ran? | Why, or why not |
> |---|---|---|
> | 1 settings and graph | | |
> | 2 generator and calibration | | |
> | 3 censoring | | |
> | 4 training stack | | |
> | 5 campaign launch | | |
> | 6 aggregation | | |
> | 7 datasheet and release | | |

**Recording the skips is the point, not the runs.** “I reviewed them and none applied” is unfalsifiable otherwise, and an unfalsifiable judgement that nothing captures is exactly the shape of the `floor_binds_rate` defect four sections down: a number nobody measured, drifting out of band with no code path able to notice. A skipped gate with a stated reason can be argued with later; a skipped gate with no record cannot.

**The walks are recorded HERE, by hand, and not in `t9v2/docs/gates/`.** That directory holds
script-written artifacts only — a file there exists because its checks ran and passed. A hand-written
walk placed among them would be indistinguishable from a measured one.

#### Gate walk — Phase A, 22 August 2026

*Phase A is the persistence and measurement work of step 2, plus the bid ladder and the ROAS gate:
commits `998ab6b` through `e7c7830`. Scoring-side only; the generator was not touched.*

| Gate | Ran? | Verdict, or why not |
|---|---|---|
| 1 settings and graph | **ran** | **PASS.** 78 nodes, 55 columns, no mismatches. 157 YAML leaves against 156: `roas_target.value` is new and the three `candidate_prices` leaves carry the widened ladder. 0 holes, 0 unsourced, undeclared count unchanged from `main`. Committed `e740b48` |
| 2 generator and calibration | skip | Its subject is byte-identical to v2's, and this is checkable rather than asserted: `git diff main..HEAD` over all seven modules `fingerprint()` hashes and over every generator YAML is empty. Only `training.yaml` changed, and **none of its nine top-level keys appears in the fingerprint's key list**, which is why the fingerprint is still `caeb2b87716e00e5`. Gate 2's own calibration is the generator's auto-calibration, not the model's |
| 3 censoring | skip | `censor.py` and the censoring settings are untouched. **The skip with an argument against it — see below** |
| 4 training stack | **ran** | **PASS, 9 of 9.** Rebuilt as one 100K seed end to end (Ken, 22 Aug), 16 seconds against 103. Running it surfaced a real defect in the gate itself, recorded below. Committed `2d84662` |
| 5 campaign launch | deferred | Cannot run without a 10M master, and it is by its own definition the launch gate for the unattended 10M run, so it belongs at step 5's campaign. `campaign.py`'s rewritten guards are covered by 13 tests in `tests/test_campaign.py` in the meantime, and the disk reserve was re-sized for the larger seed in `73db2c1` |
| 6 aggregation | skip | Needs 30 seeds. Only the zero-seed refusal changed in `stage6_aggregate.py`, and two tests cover it. Must run at the end of step 8 |
| 7 datasheet and release | skip | Nothing released |

**The Phase A gate 3 skip is a judgement, not a measurement, and is flagged as such.** The per-row eval file is
a new artifact holding `won_at_recommended`, which is derived from `lu7_competing_bid` and
`floor_price` — columns C1 and C2 cannot see. That is exactly the shape gate 3 exists to catch. The
reading taken is that it is a *scoring* artifact, that `economics` already reads the uncensored master
the same way, and that no training path reads the eval file back. One assertion would settle it
instead of arguing it: no eval-file column ever appears in a feature list. Not written.

**What running gate 4 found, which is the reason walks are worth the time.** `gate4_report.py` had
**one commit in its entire history** (`85f9824`) and so never learned Ken's 17 August amendment. It
went on judging the click-AUC floor at 100K, where it fails, which means every re-run printed FAIL and
overwrote the amendment record. The underlying trail: `85f9824` recorded the FAIL, which stood through
stages 5, 6 and 7; `47e7055` amended the rule and wrote **both** verdicts into the artifact so the
record would show a rule that was changed rather than a result that was re-scored; `38b7fe2`, twelve
hours later, collapsed that to a single PASS line and deleted both explanatory paragraphs. The
headline claim that all seven gates pass rests on the collapsed version. `2d84662` makes the floor
**reported and not gated** — the treatment install AUC's C1 and C3 readings have had from the start —
and moves the whole four-row history into the script, so a re-run reproduces the record instead of
destroying it. No number changed at any point.

#### Gate walk — Step 5, 22–23 August 2026

*The generator change. Floor fix `7aef8ff`, `k_global` re-solve `83023e4`, H5 into the machinery `5b44e67`,
the fifth encoder and leave-one-out `78f9d21`, the gate work itself `d45799b`.*

| Gate | Ran? | Verdict, or why not |
|---|---|---|
| 1 settings and graph | **ran** | **PASS.** 79 nodes, 56 columns, no mismatches. `graph.yaml` regenerated from the v2.2 documents |
| 2 generator and calibration | **ran** | **PASS at 100K and 1M.** Both regenerated after the floor fix and the re-solve; 1M's win rate is 0.299292, in band |
| 3 censoring | **ran** | **PASS, 5 of 5.** Gains the anti-leak VISIBILITY condition: `min_winning_price` absent in C1 and C2, present in C3 and C4 |
| 4 training stack | **ran** | **PASS, 10 of 10.** Gains the anti-leak FITTED-FEATURE condition: no head in any view carries the raw column |
| 5 campaign launch | deferred | Needs a 10M master, and it is the launch gate for that run. It belongs immediately before the campaign, in step 8 |
| 6 aggregation | skip | Needs 30 seeds. Runs at the end of step 8 |
| 7 datasheet and release | skip | Nothing released |

**The anti-leak check is two conditions on two gates, not one.** Visibility and use are different failures.
Gate 3 asks whether C1 and C2 can SEE `min_winning_price`; gate 4 asks whether anybody FITTED on it, including
the two views that legitimately see it. `won = 1[bid_price ≥ min_winning_price]` is an identity, so a view that
merely holds the column holds its own label, and one gate cannot cover both halves.

**Gate 4's condition was not allowed to pass by being unable to look.** Its first version read the feature
COUNTS `api.evaluate` returns, found no names to inspect, and would have reported PASS on an empty set — the
same tautology already recorded against the old leak test. `train_view` now records `t1_cols` and `t2_cols` in
its result, and a view that reports no feature lists FAILS the condition rather than being skipped.

**Four stale document pointers, all found by RUNNING the gates rather than by reading them.**
`gate_report.py`, `report_holes.py`, `make_public.py` and `tests/test_settings.py` were still reading the **v2**
register and specification, which carry 78 rows and no H5. Gate 1 reported "mismatch in nodes, emitting rows,
law T4", which reads as a graph defect and was a stale path. `make_public.py` would have **published the v2
documents beside v2.2 code**. `build_graph.py` was repointed in 5c; these are the rest of the set, and the
lesson is that repointing one caller of a forked document does not find the others.

#### Gate walk — Step 6, 23 August 2026

*The price head, `3d69914`. Scoring-side only; the generator was not touched.*

| Gate | Ran? | Verdict, or why not |
|---|---|---|
| 1 settings and graph | **ran** | **PASS.** 79 nodes, 56 columns, no mismatches. 161 YAML leaves against 157: `tier2_price` and the three `sigma` entries |
| 2 generator and calibration | **ran** | **PASS at 100K and 1M**, and run despite step 6 being scoring-side, because a comment edit had moved the fingerprint — see below |
| 3 censoring | **ran** | **PASS, 5 of 5** |
| 4 training stack | **ran** | **PASS, 10 of 10** |
| 5 campaign launch | deferred | Needs a 10M master; belongs in step 8 |
| 6 aggregation | skip | Needs 30 seeds. The price metrics have no contrast row yet, which is step 8's work |
| 7 datasheet and release | skip | Nothing released |

**A ONE-WORD COMMENT EDIT MOVED THE DESIGN FINGERPRINT and invalidated all thirty datasets.**
`network/laws.py` is one of the seven modules `fingerprint()` hashes, and "78 nodes" became "79 nodes" in a
docstring. Verified harmless rather than assumed: regenerating 100K under the new hash gives a **byte-identical
parquet**, same win rate, same `z_mu`. The fingerprint hashes source BYTES deliberately, so a law edited in
Python cannot slip past a settings-only check; the cost is that comments and whitespace fire it too, and this
is the first time that cost has been paid. Recorded, not fixed — stripping comments before hashing adds
machinery to a safety mechanism and could miss something. The practical rule is that comments in the seven
hashed modules get edited BEFORE a campaign, not during one. At 10M × 10 seeds the same slip is hours.

**One non-gating report line moved and I could not explain it from the code.** `SPEC_GAPS.md`'s undeclared list
gained `min_bid_to_win` — v1's abandoned arm, named in the Register's H5 row as history and not a config key at
all. Undeclared keys are reported and explicitly do not gate. The report's own guidance is that such entries
"should be reworded in the register so it stops being reported", which is a one-word Register change, proposed
and not made. What I could not account for is why it appeared at step 6 when the Register has not changed since
5c; recording that is better than inventing a mechanism.

#### Gate walk — Step 7, 23 August 2026

*The second bidder, `c5f63a9`. Scoring-side only.*

| Gate | Ran? | Verdict, or why not |
|---|---|---|
| 1 settings and graph | **ran** | **PASS.** 79 nodes, 56 columns, no mismatches |
| 2 generator and calibration | skip | Nothing in the generator or its settings changed |
| 3 censoring | **ran** | **PASS, 5 of 5** |
| 4 training stack | **ran** | **PASS, 10 of 10** |
| 5 campaign launch | deferred | Step 8 |
| 6 aggregation | skip | Needs 30 seeds. The two-bidder table is step 8's artifact |
| 7 datasheet and release | skip | Nothing released |

**THE SIGMA GUARD FIRED ON ITS FIRST RUN, which is the argument for having built it.** On 100K seed 20250,
contrasts formed WITHIN each bidder because levels across them mean nothing:

| Contrast | classifier | price head |
|---|---:|---:|
| win AUC C3−C1 | −0.0025 | **+0.0161** |
| profit C3/C1−1 | +1.0% | +8.3% |

The price head shows an SSP effect where the classifier shows none — the mechanism separation the step was
built for, and precisely the case v1's agreement rule would have discarded as "no claim". Then the guard,
scored at 0.75×, 1× and 1.5× σ with no refit:

| | at 0.75σ | at σ | at 1.5σ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| AUC C3−C1 | +0.0161 | +0.0161 | +0.0161 |
| profit C3/C1−1 | **−3.5%** | **+8.3%** | **+3.6%** |

**The AUC contrast is σ-robust and the profit contrast is not — it changes sign.** So one of the two is
quotable from this head and the other is not, on one seed, and the campaign settles both. That is the guard
doing exactly the job 7d assigned it, on the first data it saw.

**PHASE 3 EARNED ITS PLACE, and the campaign would have failed without it.** `run_one` had never been
exercised above 100K. The first 10M attempt reached **14.51 GB of private memory on a 15.7 GB machine, still

cause was measured rather than guessed: a `(test rows × 60)` float64 win curve is 672 MB at 10M and

minutes a seed. Disk fell from 84.7 GB free to 59.4. A 10M seed directory is 0.51 GB against the 0.53 GB
projected from 1M, so the reserve was sized correctly.

Reimplements the `t9v2-persistence` work from the trusted base, with three corrections to its design.
Nothing here touches the generator, so it runs on existing parquets and is developed at 100K and 1M.
**The numbers this step produces are scratch** — step 5 invalidates them, and every figure of record
comes from step 8.

**Order matters for three of these.** The calibration fix reads a number nothing currently records, so
the chain is: the bidder records the recommended bid, the per-row eval file stores it, and only then can
`ece_win` and `mce_win` be computed at it. The rest are independent.

| Order | | Item | What |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | New | Bidder records the recommended bid | `choose()` hands back the ladder index it took, so no tool re-derives the argmax and becomes a second implementation of the bidder it audits |
| 2 | New | Per-row eval file | Each view's predicted probabilities, EV and chosen bid written one row per auction, so a new metric costs a re-score rather than a refit |
| 3 | Fix | Calibration bid | `ece_win` and `mce_win` at the recommended bid, not the bid the generator logged. Both sides of the logged-bid diagnostic came from the data, so it never touched the bid the algorithm recommends |
| — | New | Frozen model bundles | XGBoost native JSON plus manifest, per view |
| — | New | Single training pass per seed | Four views fitted once, not twice; at 10M this is 16 minutes rather than 38 |
| — | New | Bid ladder | `geomspace(0.1, 1200, 60)` replaces `geomspace(0.1, 120, 48)`. The old ceiling clipped the argmax and put **1.528% of oracle profit on the top rung**, costing 7.24% against 0.53%. Endpoints are held by a boundary check, not fixed: profit on the top and bottom rungs must each stay under 0.1%. See the bid-ladder section below |
| — | New | ROAS gate | The bidder takes its ordinary profit-maximising bid and the row is not bid at all when `ev / b` falls below the target. A gate, not a constrained search that reprices |
| — | New | Artifact retention rule | Parquets, models and per-row eval files written and never deleted; enforced in `is_complete`, see section 5 |
| — | Fix | Fingerprint staleness guard | `is_complete` accepted a seed whatever generator built it, so thirty pre-floor-fix seeds still read complete |
| — | Fix | Aggregator on zero seeds | An empty read produced a well-formed table of n/a and wrote it over a committed result |
| — | Fix | Units test | It asserted the pre-correction value, which is why it could not catch the units defect in the first place |
| — | Fix | 1000× units bug | Every price reaching the economics is an eCPM but a won row is one impression, so summing eCPM per won row reported a thousand times the money. Only the money totals move: every ratio divides one eCPM-sum by another and the bidder's argmax is scale-invariant |

**Three design decisions taken on 22 August 2026, all departures from what the branch did.**

1. **The per-row eval file is written at evaluation, not at fit.** Training fits the four views and saves the
   bundles; evaluation then LOADS a bundle and writes the per-row eval file from it. This keeps the
   one-fit-per-seed guarantee and is stronger than the branch's design, because it puts the frozen
   artifact on the critical path: the reported numbers come from the file that shipped, so the two
   cannot silently diverge. The branch's separate in-process-versus-reloaded round-trip check becomes
   unnecessary, since evaluation scoring from the bundle IS the round trip. Only the bundle write has to
   stay inside the fitting process.
2. **ROAS defaults to target 1 and tuning is parked** (Ken, 22 Aug). Target 1 is exactly `ev / b >= 1`,
   which is profit at or above zero at the chosen rung. **Built 22 Aug in `e7c7830`, and the measurement
   corrected the expectation this paragraph originally recorded.** It said target 1 would decline nothing
   at the current ladder. That holds for the *learned* bidder and fails for the other two, and the split
   is the exact zeros. Measured on C1 of 100K seed 20250: `learned` places **1.0000** of rows, `truth_ev`
   and `oracle` place **0.2620**. Thirty percent of rows are the inactive archetype with `ev_truth` of
   exactly zero, and no bid returns a target of 1 on a row worth nothing; the rest are worth less than
   the cheapest rung. The learned head cannot produce an exact zero — its smallest prediction is 4.83 eCPM
   against a bottom rung of 0.1 — so the gate never fires on it. **Inert where the plan expected it to
   bite, live where it expected nothing.** Nothing reported moves: the learned profits are 38.119, 44.012,
   36.738 and 40.896 before and after, and the oracle ceiling rises from 246.032 to 246.034 by declining
   18 wins that were together losing 0.002. It rises rather than falls because a declined row is by
   construction one whose bid exceeded its own value. The sweep that would use the gate is therefore
   margin discipline rather than declining hopeless rows, and it is queued as **Q2** below.
3. **The calibration fix is written now and tested in two parts.** Its real-data check waits for the next
   regeneration, because the per-row eval files the branch produced were destroyed with the masters.
   But a unit test over a dozen synthetic rows with known probabilities and known bids ships WITH the
   change, needs no generated data, and catches the wiring. The precedent is `7557c41`, which shipped
   the units fix without its test and was committed red; `938f28c6` exists only to repair that.

#### Step 3. Feature design — paper only — SETTLED 22 August 2026

**The quantity is `min_winning_price`, and it is `max(LU7, floor)` on every row.**

**This reverses the 21 August position and reinstates v1's arm B1.** The section below still argues
for the exact second-highest bid over the clipped `max(LU7, floor)`, on the ground that the clipped
form loses information whenever the floor binds. That argument is withdrawn. The information it loses
has no consumer: the bidder needs `max(LU7, floor)` and nothing finer, so LU7's value below a binding
floor is never used. What the clipped form buys in exchange is decisive — **nothing is censored**.

| Row class | Share | `min_winning_price` | Observable before this change |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Won | 29.9% | `max(LU7, floor)` | **no** — only `LU7 ≤ bid` |
| Lost, bid cleared the floor, sold | 41.8% | LU7 | yes, as `winning_price` |
| Lost, bid below the floor, sold | 16.6% | LU7 | yes, as `winning_price` |
| Lost, unsold | 11.7% | **the floor exactly**, since `LU7 < floor` | yes, but only as a bound before |

70.1% was already observable to C3 and C4. The change adds the won rows and turns the unsold bound
into a point, taking the target to **100% observed**. That is what makes step 6 a clean switch to
plain regression rather than a hybrid carrying a censored tail.

**Carry the B1 caveat.** v1 ran arm B1, the won-rows-only clipped form, and it did not move
overpayment: −0.8% [−2.6, +1.0], paired across ten seeds (`docs/KDD_Paper_Draft_v2.md:517`). This
construct covers every row rather than won rows only, and v2.2's target is ranking rather than
overpayment, so the finding does not transfer directly. It is recorded because the closest prior test
came back empty.

**One column, not two.** An intermediate design carried a separate `top_rival_bid_observed` holding
LU7 wherever the impression sold. It is subsumed: its won-row content is `min_winning_price`'s won-row
content, and on lost-sold rows the two are equal. `winning_price` stays unchanged beside the new
column — it is a real market fact, the existing encoders read it, and removing it would move v2's
baseline.

**LU7 stays latent, and the write-up must say what that means.** "Latent" in the register is a
COLUMN-level claim: `lu7_competing_bid` is never emitted. It is not a claim that the value is
unknowable, and C3 and C4 already recover LU7 exactly on the 58.4% of rows where they lost and the
impression sold, under the name `winning_price`. Stating this plainly is what stops a reader
concluding the price head is trained on ground truth.

**The anti-leak rule, and why it is stricter here than for `winning_price`.** `won = bid ≥ max(LU7,
floor)` means `won = bid ≥ min_winning_price` is an IDENTITY, not an approximation. Handed this column
per row, the win classifier does not merely improve, it reproduces its own label. So the column joins
`SETTLEMENT_COLS` beside `winning_price` and `bid_density` and reaches the classifier only as cell
history through an encoder. The gate must prove no head carries it among its features, per view. Note
that nothing checks this today: section 5 records that the serving whitelist was never built, so
nothing compares a model's feature manifest against its view's visible columns.

**The encoder consequence, which may be the larger half of the change.** `_enc_ssp_lost_price` exists
only because the declared SSP encoder is diluted: on won rows `winning_price` is our own bid, a number
C1 already holds, so about 30% of that encoder's mass carries nothing new. An encoder over
`min_winning_price` averages a genuine market price on 100% of rows, against `_enc_ssp_price`'s 70% and
`_enc_ssp_lost_price`'s 58%. **Approved by Ken, 22 August 2026.** It repairs the dilution at source rather than working around it, and
`_enc_ssp_lost_price` may then retire — to be tested at step 5, not assumed.

#### Step 4. Encoder-key diagnostic — PARKED 22 August 2026

**Ken: it is only a test, its result might change nothing, and time is short.** Parked, not cancelled.

What it would have tested: the SSP price history reaches the win model as shrunken cell means keyed by
`(app_id, slot_format, ad_exchange, daypart)`, while the rival private structure varies along two axes that
key does not contain — LR2 by `(os × device)` segment and LR3 by day. Whatever those axes put into prices is
averaged away before the model sees it, so part of the SSP null may be a representation failure rather than an
absence of signal.

**The consequence of parking it, stated so it is not discovered later.** The new encoder at step 5 inherits the
existing key by default rather than by evidence. If the key is the thing suppressing the signal, H5's encoder
will suppress it too, and a null at step 8 will not distinguish "the price information is not there" from
"the key averages it away". That is a live alternative explanation for any null this study reports, and it
belongs in the limitations rather than in the results.

#### Step 5. Generator change — the one regeneration — SETTLED 22 August 2026

The only step that invalidates data. Two things change the generator: the floor fix and the new column. They are
batched here so the campaign is paid once. Everything else in v2.2 runs against data already on disk.

**Code sites below are named by SYMBOL, with a line number only as a hint.** Line numbers drift the moment anything above them is edited, and a plan that says "line 43" after the file has moved on is worse than one that says nothing, because it still reads as precise. Search for the named constant, function or literal; if the line agrees, good, and if it does not, the symbol is still right.

##### 5a. The floor fix

**Both iPinYou price shapes are normalised by the PAYING median. Neither is divided by its own.** The floor and
the paying price are two prices in one market, and what carries the market's structure is the ratio between them.
Dividing each by its own median forces both to 1 and erases it. The paying median is the right denominator
because the target both shapes multiply, `T^ecpm`, is itself a clearing-price benchmark, so `ψ^clearing · T^ecpm`
must land on it.

Measured: the floor pmf's weighted median is 40, the paying pmf's is 70, so the correct floor shape has median
**0.571** and the buggy one has median 1, inflating every floor by **70/40 = 1.750**.

| | buggy | correct | v1 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| P(bid < floor) | 0.391 | 0.283 | 0.300 |
| P(floor > LU7) | 0.330 | 0.212 | 0.231 |
| P(unsold \| lost) | 0.335 | 0.167 | 0.167 |
| shape ratio | 0.991 | 0.566 | 0.566 |

**Why it flatters C1, which is the reason it must not ship.** An inflated floor turns a third of the market into
rows where the floor already exceeds our bid — a certain loss decidable from two columns every view holds. C1's
win AUC falls **0.8720 to 0.8195** once those free wins disappear. It also moves Tier 1, unexpectedly: C1 and C3
learn the funnel from won rows only, so changing the floor changes which rows they train on.

**Reimplement, do not cherry-pick `cec5396`.** Two lines in `price_shapes()`: drop the floor's own median and
divide both by the paying one. The commit also edits `calibrated.yaml`, the v2 plan and `tools/roas_sweep.py`,
the last of which does not exist on this branch. Copy its replacement docstring verbatim.

**The regression test asserts the medians, not the ratio.** `_weighted_median(pay) == 1.0` and
`_weighted_median(floor) == 40.0/70.0`, exact equality. `cec5396`'s reported 0.5664 is the realised MEAN ratio
over drawn rows and would fail as an assertion.

**Two documentation errors were corrected alongside it, both about this same normalisation.** The Specification's
1.6 table said "about 57 percent of floors are zero"; the measured zero atom is **14.15 percent**, and 57 percent
was the shape ratio 40/70 misread as a share. The Node Register fixed that number on 16 August 2026 and the
Specification did not follow. Both files now also state the denominator explicitly rather than saying "median
normalised", which is what allowed the code to diverge without contradicting anything written down.

##### 5b. Re-solving `k_global`

**`k_global` is re-solved, and it runs BEFORE the campaign, not after it.**

`k_global` is the global multiplier on our own bid, `bid = k_global · k_cpa(tier) · v_slot · ease · eltv_b2 ·
shade · noise`. Nobody picks its value. A bisection finds whatever makes the win rate land on **0.30**, the
target at `market.yaml` `win_rate.target`, within a tolerance of 0.005. The floor is half the win hurdle, `won = bid ≥
max(LU7, floor)`, so cutting every floor by 1.75 times makes the same bids clear more often and the calibration
breaks. The solver pulls `k_global` down to compensate: **1.376914063 → 1.09621**, achieving 0.29904.

**The ordering matters and inverts the obvious one.** `k_global` is an INPUT to generation, not a measurement
taken from it. Generate the thirty datasets first and every one of them carries the old bid scale, permanently.
The solve therefore comes first — and it needs no dataset of its own, because the solver draws its own warm-up
sample.

| | Step 5's internal order |
|---:|---|
| 1 | Floor fix, the H5 law, and the rest of step 5's code and settings changes |
| 2 | `python -m t9v2.autocal --only k_global` — draws **200,000 rows at 1M pools**, measures the win rate, bisects |
| 3 | Check the answer against 1.09621; write it to `calibrated.yaml` |
| 4 | **Then** the campaign generates the thirty datasets |

**Solve at 1M pools, not at 100K, and the reason is not cost.** The entity pools scale with the profile —
22,000 users and 150 apps at 100K against 220,000 and 500 at 1M — so a `k_global` solved on 100K would be tuned
to a market composition that exists only at 100K, and the 1M and 10M campaigns would then miss the target. The
solver's declared setting, 200,000 rows at 1M pools, is a small draw against full-size pools: as cheap as a 100K
run, but measuring the market the campaign will actually produce. That this works is visible in v2's own output,
where one `k_global` gives win rates of 0.29976, 0.29973 and 0.29977 across the three scales.

**Treat the answer as a check, not just a value.** It must land within 1% of **1.096208496**, which is what
`cec5396` reached at an achieved win rate of 0.29904. H5 is a pure function of draws that already exist and
consumes no randomness, and the bid ladder is a scoring setting that never reaches the generator, so the floor
fix is step 5's ONLY behavioural change. If the solver returns something else, something unintended has moved
and the right response is to diagnose it rather than accept the number.

##### 5c. Regenerating `graph.yaml`, and the one edit that fails silently

`config/graph.yaml` is GENERATED and never hand-edited. `tools/build_graph.py` reads the Node Register and the
Specification and writes it, so adding H5 to the documents changes nothing until the tool is re-run. Two things
come out of that re-run. The column enters the machinery — H5's node block, and `min_winning_price` in
`column_order`, which is what `censor.py` reads to know the column is C3/C4-only and what startup check V4
compares the emitting rows against. And **the design fingerprint changes**, which is exactly what marks the
thirty existing datasets stale, and what `is_complete` will use at step 8 to refuse to reuse them.

Three edits are required first, or the re-run does the wrong thing:

| Site | Change | Fails how |
|---|---|---|
| `REG` and `SPEC` in `build_graph.py` (~L21-22) | `REG` and `SPEC` repointed at the v2.2 filenames | loudly — it would otherwise read the v2 documents, which have no H5 |
| the `frozen_columns()` regex in `build_graph.py` (~L152) | the regex `r"55 columns\):"` becomes `56` | loudly — it parses the count out of a literal Specification sentence and raises when the match fails |
| **`SSP_ONLY_NODES`** in `build_graph.py` (~L43) | **`SSP_ONLY_NODES = {"H4", "H5", "H9"}`** | **SILENTLY** |

**Only the third is dangerous, and it is the single highest-risk edit in v2.2.** `observability()` decides a
node's censoring by testing, in order: no columns, then `HIDDEN_NODES`, then a role beginning "latent" or
"estimand", then `SSP_ONLY_NODES`, then a role beginning "outcome", then everything else falls through to
`ALL_VIEWS`. H5's role string is "observable (SSP-visible, C3 and C4 only)", which matches none of the earlier
tests — **the role text is never parsed for the words "SSP-visible"**. So without H5 in that set the tool
succeeds, writes a well-formed `graph.yaml`, and gives `min_winning_price` all four views while `winning_price`
stays correctly SSP-only. C1 and C2 then receive the exact hurdle, `won = 1[bid ≥ min_winning_price]` becomes an
identity they can read, and the SSP contrast collapses to zero with no number anywhere looking wrong.

The banner strings at `:7`, `:202` and `:210` carry "78 generator variables" and "the frozen 55"; `:210` is
written into `graph.yaml` as a header comment, so leaving it stale puts a false count inside the generated file.

**Verified by dry run, 22 August 2026.** The v2.2 register parses to **79 nodes, 56 columns**, with H5 at index
67 between H2 and H3, and the v2.2 Specification's column list parses to exactly 56 entries with
`min_winning_price` present, immediately after `winning_price`.

##### 5d. The fifth encoder, and the leave-one-out it cannot ship without

**`_enc_ssp_minwin_price`, a fifth `PriceEncoder` over `min_winning_price`.** Same cell key as the other four,
`(app_id, slot_format, ad_exchange, daypart)`, same shared shrink `k = 20`, and it averages EVERY training row
because the column is never NaN. Present in C3 and C4 only, because the column is. It reaches the win
classifier; the price head's whitelist excludes every SSP encoder by construction, so nothing has to be wired
to keep it out, and that is what keeps the price head's feature list identical across all four views.

**It exists because the encoder it sits beside is diluted, and the dilution is the whole reason the feature is
worth adding.** Under first-price clearing `winning_price` on a WON row is our own bid, a number C1 already
holds in `bid_price`. So the declared SSP encoder averages a mixture, and only its lost-sold rows carry a price
the DSP could not otherwise know. Measured on 1M seed 20250:

| Encoder | Rows averaged | Carrying a genuine rival price |
|---|---:|---:|
| `_enc_ssp_price` | 76.5%, every cleared row | **46.6%** |
| `_enc_ssp_lost_price` | 46.6%, lost-and-sold only | 46.6% |
| **`_enc_ssp_minwin_price`** | **100%** | **100%** |

`_enc_ssp_lost_price` was added at stage 4 as a workaround for exactly this dilution: it drops the won rows
because they tell the model nothing new. The new encoder repairs it at source instead. On a won row
`min_winning_price` is the runner-up threshold, which is precisely the quantity a DSP without SSP integration
never learns, and the only row class where the old feed was worthless becomes the one where the new one earns
its place.

**`_enc_ssp_lost_price` STAYS in this build.** Retirement is decided by evidence, not by the argument above
being persuasive. The two are not the same estimator — one is a selected mean over lost-sold rows, the other an
unselected mean over all rows — so retire it only if a paired ten-seed ablation at 1M puts the 95% interval on
Δ win AUC inside [−0.0005, +0.0005].

**LEAVE-ONE-OUT IS MANDATORY, ON ALL FIVE ENCODERS.** This is the highest-risk item in v2.2 and the reason is
that `won = 1[bid ≥ min_winning_price]` is an identity. The cell AVERAGE is legitimate history and is what the
SSP layer really supplies. But `build()` fits on the training split and `apply()` then runs over the whole
frame, so on a training row the row's own value sits inside its own cell mean. Measured: the median cell holds
4 training rows at 100K and 9 at 1M, with 91% and 72% of cells under twenty. Against `k = 20` a row's own
weight is `1/(count + k)` —

| cell count | 1 | 4 | 9 | 20 | 55 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| own-row weight | 4.8% | 4.2% | 3.4% | 2.5% | 1.3% |

— so the shrinkage holds it near 4% rather than the 25% a raw mean would give. **Four percent of an ordinary
feature is nothing. Four percent of a column that equals the label is not**, and the failure mode is silent:
nothing crashes, no number looks wrong, and C3 and C4 quietly receive a contaminated estimate of their own win
boundary. That would manufacture the SSP win-AUC lift v2's entire rebuild established was an artifact, and it
would reverse RQ2's answer.

So the encoder gains a `transform_train` that subtracts the row's own contribution, cell and parent alike,
before scoring a training row, and it is applied to all five emitted columns rather than only the new one. The
arithmetic must not be trusted on its own: gate 4's fitted-feature condition tests it empirically, and the suite carries a
backstop that force-adds the raw column to a C3 fit and asserts win AUC ≥ 0.999, so the exclusion is shown to
be load-bearing rather than merely present.

#### Step 6. Survival → plain regression — SETTLED 22 August 2026

**One estimand for all four views: `m_i^win`, the minimum winning price.** What differs between views is not
what is predicted but how well it is observed, which is the ablation working as intended rather than a
methodological difference smuggled in beside it.

| View | What it can state about `m_i^win` | Observation |
|---|---|---|
| C3, C4 | the value, from the `min_winning_price` column | **exact, every row** |
| C1, C2 — won | `floor ≤ m_i^win ≤ bid` — the floor is visible in every view | bounded interval |
| C1, C2 — lost | `m_i^win ≥ max(bid, floor)`, the bound **closed** | right-unbounded interval |

**The lower bound on lost rows is closed, and writing it open would be wrong on 11.7% of rows.** Losing
means `bid < m_i^win`, which alone gives an open bound at the bid. But `m_i^win ≥ floor` always, and on an
unsold row `LU7 < floor`, so `m_i^win` equals the floor EXACTLY. Where the bid is under the floor the
binding constraint is therefore the floor, attained rather than exceeded, and an open bound would exclude
the true value on every unsold row. XGBoost's `label_lower_bound` is closed by convention, so the
arithmetic `max(bid, floor)` is right; it is the notation that had to be fixed.

**Why C1 and C2 keep a censored model, in Ken's words (22 Aug): a real DSP without SSP integration simply does
not have the luxury of training a price head on observed prices.** That is exactly the deprivation the ablation
exists to measure, so the censored likelihood is not a workaround, it is the condition.

**The interval is built by one function and guarded by one test, not materialised as a column.** Ken
raised the obvious worry: arithmetic done on the fly inside the trainer is exactly the kind of thing that
goes quietly wrong. The answer is not a column. An interval is TWO numbers, so it would take two of them,
and `mwp_upper` is finite precisely when `won = 1`, making it the Tier-2 label in disguise and something
that would itself need banning from every feature list. Materialising the censoring boundary into the
master invites the leak it is meant to prevent.

So: one function, `mwp_bounds(df) -> (lower, upper)`, in one place —

| row | lower | upper |
|---|---|---|
| won | `floor_price` | `bid_price` |
| lost | `max(bid_price, floor_price)` | `+inf` |

— and a test that asserts `lower ≤ max(LU7, floor) ≤ upper` on **every row in every view**, checked
against the master where both `LU7` and the floor are known. That verifies the property rather than
storing the result, and any arithmetic slip fails it immediately. A column could not be checked this way:
it would simply hold whatever the same arithmetic produced.

**The feature list is identical in all four views, and that is what makes this step's contrast readable.**
The price head takes the base columns minus `bid_price`, plus `_enc_dsp_price`, and nothing else —
enforced by a raise in `price.features()` rather than by convention. Two exclusions carry the design:

- **`bid_price` is dropped** because it IS the label's censoring boundary. Given it as a feature, the model
  learns to predict just under the bid on won rows and just over on lost ones, memorising the censoring
  pattern instead of the price. It still enters at SCORING time as the point at which the curve is
  evaluated, which is a different role entirely.
- **The SSP encoders are dropped** because they exist only in C3 and C4. Including them would make the
  price head's features differ by view, and its `C3 − C1` gap would then mix features with labels. The DSP
  encoder is kept precisely because it exists everywhere, so it preserves the symmetry while still carrying
  real information about what a cell clears at.

This is the division of labour between the two Tier-2 heads: **the classifier varies features and holds the
target fixed; the price head varies the label and holds features fixed.** A `C3 − C1` gap on the classifier
means the price history was informative. The same gap on the price head means label quality was. Each head
holds the other axis constant, which is what makes the two mechanisms separable rather than confounded.

**One likelihood, not two.** The four views share one interval-censored model class. C3 and C4 supply degenerate
intervals `[x, x]`, C1 and C2 supply real ones. This removes what would otherwise be a confound: with plain
regression on one side and a censored model on the other, `C3 − C1` would mix the data layer with the estimator,
and no reader could tell which produced the contrast. With one class, the estimator is held constant by
construction and the contrast is the data alone.

So the step's original title is now the wrong description of it. The move is not survival-to-plain-regression
across the board. It is **the same censored regression throughout, with C3 and C4's intervals collapsed to
points by the new column**.

**This halves the sigma problem rather than dissolving it, which corrects what this document said at step 3.**
For AFT with a normal error and all-exact observations, the location MLE does not depend on the scale, so σ
stops affecting C3 and C4's predictions entirely. For interval observations it does affect them, because the
likelihood is a difference of two normal CDFs whose shape σ sets. C1 and C2 are interval throughout. **σ
therefore still sits on the C3 − C1 contrast, through C1.** An unjustified constant on the study's headline
number is exactly the defect recorded against `t9v2-two-bidders`, so it still has to be answered — it is simply
now a question about the censored side alone, where it is at least identifiable from the data rather than
copied from v1.

**σ is read off C3's residuals, and the reason it is nearly free is the same fact that makes it inert
there.** Because σ does not affect the fit when labels are exact, C3's price head can be fitted with any
placeholder and the residual spread read off afterwards:

```
sigma_hat = std( log(m^win) − log(pred) )      # C3, held-out rows
```

That value becomes C1 and C2's `aft_loss_distribution_scale`. The whole cost is **one ordering rule** —
C3 trains before C1 and C2 in the view loop — **and one line of arithmetic**. No search, no pilot run, no
extra model fit. Two guards ride with it: clamp `sigma_hat` to [0.2, 2.0] so a pathological seed cannot
produce nonsense, and record it in `results.json` per seed so it is visible rather than silent.

**Do not estimate it at one scale and apply it at another.** Residual spread shrinks as the model improves
with more data, so a value taken from a 1M pilot would be too wide for a 10M campaign. Estimate within each
run, at its own scale.

**The cost of this choice, stated because a reader should be told rather than left to find it.** C1's σ is
derived from C3's labels, so a view that is defined by not having SSP data borrows one quantity computed
from it. Three options were weighed and each costs something: estimating per view puts a free parameter
directly on the headline contrast, which is worse; deriving σ from the rival-bid law gives the raw
dispersion of prices, which is an upper bound on residual spread rather than the value. The chosen option
transfers a nuisance parameter, not price information — C1 borrows a scale, and nothing about where prices
sit — and it is the only one of the three that leaves the contrast free of a fitted parameter. It belongs
in the limitations.

**σ ≈ 0.9 IS A TEMPORARY VALUE, and the PROCEDURE is the decision** (Ken, 23 August 2026). Option B stands —
read the scale off C3's residuals — and it stands on measurement rather than on the argument above, because the
alternative was tested and lost. A better value is queued as **Q3**. The procedure is reproducible: it returns
0.9024 at 100K and 0.8911 at 1M, a 1.3 percent move over ten times the data.

*Three corrections to this section, each from measuring what it asserted.*

**"σ stops affecting C3 and C4's predictions entirely" is too strong.** That claim is about the analytic MLE
and is right about it. A BOOSTED AFT is not a pure MLE: σ scales the gradients, so it moves both the split
choices and the early-stopping point. Measured on C3 at 100K, rmse_log runs 0.9136 · 0.9084 · 0.9089 · 0.9088 ·
0.9081 · 0.9060 across σ = 0.2 to 4.0 — **0.0076 over a twentyfold span.** A real response rather than scatter,
since the head is deterministic at 0.0000 spread over five model seeds, and negligible for any purpose here.
Read the sentence as "negligibly", not "entirely".

**The alternative was tested and is worse.** C1 can estimate σ from its OWN censored likelihood, using nothing
it is not entitled to, and it picks 0.44 against C3's 0.9024. That is not a better answer: C1's rmse is
**2.8981** at 0.44 against **1.2554** at 0.9024. The criterion is blind exactly where it must see — C1's
validation nloglik moves only 0.568 to 0.578 across the whole range while its accuracy swings 1.00 to 2.90, and
the likelihood minimum lands on the worst accuracy in the window. **σ is weakly identified from interval
data**, because 70 percent of C1's rows say only "at least this much". *Arguably a finding rather than a
defect: a DSP without SSP integration cannot reliably calibrate its own uncertainty either, which is this
study's deprivation showing up in a second place.*

**The transfer is a defensible SOURCE, not a derivation.** C3's residual spread and C1's likelihood scale are
different quantities that share units. C1 predicts worse than C3, so if σ tracked residual spread C1 would want
a LARGER value; its accuracy optimum is 0.50, smaller. The heuristic does not land on C1's optimum, and nothing
legitimate does — 0.50 is reachable only by minimising C1's error against `m^win`, which C1 never observes, so
choosing it would leak SSP information through the hyperparameter.

**The contrast's dependence on σ must be REPORTED, and that is the part currently missing.** At 100K seed 20250
the price contrast reads −0.0887 at σ = 0.5, **−0.3466** at the derived 0.9024, −0.4710 at 1.0 and −1.5666 at
2.0. The floor near **−0.09** is the irreducible cost of only ever seeing intervals; everything above it is the
cost of a nuisance parameter C1 cannot set for itself. Reporting the derived figure beside that floor tells a
reader what the transfer costs; reporting one alone does not. Folded into step 8.

**Still open here:** nothing, given Q3. **Step 6 is CLOSED, 23 August 2026.**

#### Step 7. Second bidder — SETTLED 22 August 2026

**Where the price head is already specified, so this section does not restate it.** Duplication is how
`ev_ratio` came to name two quantities, so each fact lives in one place.

| For | See |
|---|---|
| The head's target, labels, objective, feature whitelist and σ | **step 6** |
| The fifth encoder and its leave-one-out | **5d** |
| The 60-rung ladder both bidders and the oracle share | **the bid ladder section** |
| How the head becomes a BIDDER, how the two are scored alike, and how they are reported | here |

**What the second bidder is for.** v2 had one Tier-2 head, a classifier on `won`. Specification 1.5 makes
`won` visible in ALL FOUR views, so C1 and C3 fit the same model on the same label over the same rows and the
only thing that can differ between them is features. Every SSP economic contrast in v2 was therefore null **by
construction rather than by finding**. The price head predicts `m^win`, which C3 and C4 observe exactly and C1
and C2 only bound, so SSP value can now enter through LABEL quality as well. That is the point of the step.

**It is not a better bidder, and its levels must never be compared.** The two heads produce different win
curves, so they choose different bids, so they win different impressions. Their profit LEVELS are therefore
not comparable and must not be put beside each other as though they were. Only contrasts computed WITHIN a
bidder are comparable, and then only by sign and verdict. v1 learned this the hard way: its AFT bidder showed
higher profit in every cell and that was never evidence of anything.

##### 7a. From a price prediction to a bid

The head predicts `m̂`, the location of a lognormal over `m^win`. That distribution IS a win curve, because the
win rule is `won = bid ≥ max(LU7, floor)` and both the bid and the floor are visible in every view:

```
P(win | b) = Φ( (log b − log m̂) / σ ) · 1[b ≥ floor]
```

**The floor term is not v1's and its absence there was a defect.** v1's AFT never saw `floor_price`, so its
curve was the Φ alone and it put positive win probability on bids that cannot win at all. That is part of why
v1's AFT bidder overpaid two to three times its classifier. The floor is observable in every view, so
including it costs nothing and is simply the win rule written down.

**Monotone by construction**, unlike the classifier's curve. `m̂` does not depend on `b`, Φ increases, and the
indicator is a single step up, so the product is non-decreasing in the bid on every row with no reliance on
what the trees learned. The classifier needs `monotone_constraints {bid_price: 1}` to get the same property.

The bid itself is then the same argmax the classifier uses, over the same ladder:
`argmax_b (ev − b) · P(win | b)`.

##### 7b. One σ, three consumers, and the oracle exempt

σ has three functional consumers: the AFT fit, the win curve, and the point scorer used for `auc_win`. **All
three take the one value step 6 estimates from C3's residuals.** `price.SIGMA = 1.0`, copied from v1 and
justified nowhere, is deleted from the module; σ becomes a fitted quantity carried per seed, not a constant.

**The oracle never sees σ.** Its curve stays the exact step `1[b ≥ m^win]`, unsmoothed, one ceiling shared by
both bidders so `value_vs_oracle` divides both by the same thing. A first-price win rule is deterministic. v1
smoothed its oracle with `AFT_SCALE`, which made the ceiling a function of the same arbitrary constant the
bidder used, and v2 fixed that deliberately; it must not be undone here.

##### 7c. Scoring the two heads alike

Both heads are scored on the same rows against the same labels, or the comparison means nothing.

| Metric | At which bid | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `auc_win` | the **logged** bid | `won` is the outcome at the bid the row actually carried. Scoring at per-row recommended bids would pair each score with a label from a different counterfactual |
| `ece_win`, `mce_win` | the **recommended** bid, placed rows only | This is the correction step 2 makes: calibration matters where the bidder operates, not where the generator happened to bid |

Both are emitted under `heads.win` and `heads.win_price` with the same key names, and the calibration keys are
suffixed `_at_recommended` and `_at_logged` rather than reusing the bare `ece_win`, which means the logged bid
in v2's thirty committed `results.json` files.

##### 7d. How the two are reported — judged on merit, not gated by agreement

**Ken, 22 August 2026: results are judged on their merit. The v1 rule that only claims agreeing across both
heads may be quoted is NOT adopted.** It is recorded here with why, because the reasoning behind it is sound
and the reason for departing from it is specific.

v1 adopted that rule after its own headline died of the lack of one: a "+6.5 percent overpayment reduction,
10 of 10 seeds" that vanished under the classifier bidder and is recorded in v1's files as an AFT artifact.
The lesson — that one head's assumptions can manufacture a result — is real and is not in dispute.

**But a blanket veto is the wrong instrument here, because the two heads do not measure the same thing.** The
classifier's `C3 − C1` can move only through FEATURES, since its target is visible in every view. The price
head's can move only through LABELS, since its features are identical in every view. That separation is
deliberate and is the whole design. So a disagreement is not noise cancelling a claim; it is potentially the
most informative result the study can produce. "SSP improves the label a price model can learn from, and does
not improve the features a win classifier reads" is a finding about WHERE the value of an SSP integration
lies. Under an agreement rule it would be discarded as "no claim" — throwing away exactly the signal the
second head was built to generate.

So the reporting rule is:

- **Both heads are always reported**, side by side, for all three contrasts and every metric.
- **A disagreement is described, not suppressed.** State which head moved, in which direction, and which
  mechanism that implicates — features or labels.
- **No head is nominated primary in advance**, and none needs to be. What each measures is stated instead.
- **The narrow risk the v1 rule guarded against gets a targeted guard**, since it is real: any claim resting
  on the price head must be shown insensitive to σ. Re-score the contrast at σ̂ and at σ̂ × [0.75, 1.5] and
  report whether the verdict holds. This costs no refit — σ enters only the curve and the scorer, not the fit.

**The mechanics that compute all this belong to step 8, not here.** Forming `C3 − C1` means pairing across
ten seeds and putting an interval on the difference, which is aggregation — stage 6's job in the seven-stage
scheme. What step 7 owns is the per-seed scoring that feeds it, and the rule above for reading the result.
One thing does belong here because it is a property of the two heads rather than of the aggregator: **profit
contrasts are reported as a percentage of that bidder's own baseline, never as dollars set beside the other
bidder's**, for the incomparable-levels reason above.

##### 7e. Persistence

The price head joins the frozen bundle: schema `t9v2-bundle-1` becomes `t9v2-bundle-2`, gaining
`tier2/price.ubj` and a `model.price` block. **σ is a mandatory manifest field** — `load_bundle` raises when it
is absent rather than falling back to a default, because σ sets the curve width, the width sets the chosen bid,
and a bundle that silently rebuilt the curve at the wrong width would produce plausible wrong economics. Today
`bundle.py` has zero references to the price head, so a fitted AFT dies with its process and any new metric
costs a full retrain.

#### Step 8. Campaign and reporting — PARTIAL, the two-bidder aggregation only

**Settled, 22 August 2026**, in 8a to 8h below. Two items were considered and DROPPED rather than
deferred: widening the tilt sweep's coverage, and unifying the three confidence-interval
implementations. One remains open: `RATIO_FLOOR`, which only bites once step 2's units fix lands and
is recorded at the end of 8e.

##### 8a. The two-bidder contrast table

Three contrasts (C2−C1, C3−C1, C4−C2) × five metrics (profit, `value_captured`, `value_vs_oracle`, wins,
`auc_win`) × two bidders = **30 cells**, written to `t9v2/docs/gates/agreement_<scale>.{md,json}`.

Per cell: paired-by-seed mean, 95% interval, sign count, and a verdict of POSITIVE, NEGATIVE or NULL. Read
under step 7d's rule — both heads always reported, disagreements described rather than suppressed, no head
primary.

**The artifact is always written and the build never fails on a disagreement.** A finding must never be able
to suppress its own evidence. The release check asserts only that the file exists and covers all thirty cells.

**Profit contrasts are percentages of that bidder's own baseline**, never dollars set beside the other
bidder's, because the two heads win different impressions and their levels are not comparable.

**σ sensitivity rides along**, since step 7d requires any price-head claim to survive it: each price-head cell
is recomputed at σ̂ × 0.75 and σ̂ × 1.5 and the verdict at each is reported beside the headline one. No refit —
σ enters the curve and the scorer, not the fit.

##### 8b. Retention: nothing under `output/` is ever deleted

**Approved 22 August 2026, as insurance rather than as a repair.** Audited this session: the only deletion
calls anywhere in `t9v2/src` and `t9v2/tools` are in `make_public.py`, and they clear the RELEASE copy under
`release/`, never `output/`. `T9_DELETE_PARQUET` does not exist on this branch. The single offender,
`run_arm1.py`, lives only on the abandoned branches and is not being reimplemented.

**What it cost when it did happen.** `run_arm1.py` deleted each master parquet after using it, which destroyed
the parquets, models and per-row eval files behind the corrected 1M results. Those numbers survive only because
their markdown was committed, now tagged `v2-corrected-1M`, and re-deriving the data is a checkout plus a full
1M campaign.

**Two mechanisms, and the completeness rule is the stronger one.**

| | Catches a deletion | When it speaks |
|---|---|---|
| The completeness rule (8c) | yes, and **self-heals** — a missing artifact makes the seed incomplete, so the campaign regenerates it | the next campaign run |
| The no-delete test | yes, prevents rather than repairs | the moment the line is written |

Completeness does the real work. Its gap is timing: it only speaks when a campaign runs, and what actually
happened in August was a deletion followed by nobody running a campaign against that data again, so the loss
sat undetected until it mattered.

**So the test is kept, and the reason is not the past offender.** Steps 5 to 8 add several new tools —
the ladder boundary check, the encoder ablation, the reporting rewrite — and a cleanup line in a fresh script
written under time pressure is exactly how this recurs. `t9v2/tests/test_retention.py` walks the AST of every
module under `t9v2/src` and `t9v2/tools` and fails if any `unlink`, `os.remove` or `shutil.rmtree` call can
target a path under `output/`. One allowlisted exception, the bundle directory rebuild inside a seed's own run.

**No opt-in flag is added.** `T9_DELETE_PARQUET` is not reintroduced under any name: an opt-in is what gets
opted into, and disk pressure at 2am is when it would be.

##### 8c. Completeness: what makes a seed done

`is_complete(scale, seed, fingerprint)`, with the fingerprint **required and no default**. A seed counts as
done only when every artifact below exists, parses, and records a design fingerprint equal to the current one:

- the master parquet and its `.manifest.json`
- `results.json`, covering all four views
- one frozen bundle per view
- one per-row eval file per view

**The live code checks none of this.** `campaign.py`'s `is_complete(scale, seed)` today asks only whether
`results.json` parses and names four views — no parquet, no manifest, no bundles, no per-row file and no
fingerprint. That is precisely how thirty pre-floor-fix seeds would read complete and a v2.2 campaign would
skip all of them in a second, then republish v2's numbers under a v2.2 heading with the gate passing.

The rule is already written in this document's section 5 and step 2, and in `CLAUDE.md`. Until step 8 lands it
is a promise the code does not keep.

##### 8d. The leak test, cut back to the one part that earns its place

**Ken, 22 August 2026: the exclusion mechanism already exists, so the elaborate test is not built.** Verified
against the code before cutting it: all three feature builders — `tier1_features`, `tier2_features` and the
price head's own `features()` — funnel through `F.base_columns`, which removes `ALL_OUTCOME_COLS`,
`SETTLEMENT_COLS`, `NEVER` and anything beginning `_enc_`. **One line does the work**: `min_winning_price`
joins `SETTLEMENT_COLS`. A proposal to assert the exclusion across four views and six heads, reading each
FITTED model's own feature list, was rejected as restating one funnel six times.

**What is built instead is a single backstop, and it is documentation rather than protection.**

> `test_the_leak_would_be_catastrophic` — fit the win classifier on a C3 frame with `min_winning_price`
> force-ADDED, on about 20,000 rows, and assert win AUC ≥ 0.999. Beside it, the ordinary C3 fit asserts
> ≤ 0.95.

The ordinary exclusion test proves the column is absent. It says nothing about whether absence matters. This
one proves the ban is load-bearing, so a maintainer tidying `SETTLEMENT_COLS` a year from now finds out what
the column does rather than seeing a name with no stated reason. `won = 1[bid ≥ min_winning_price]` is an
identity, so the model does not learn the market from it, it solves for the label.

**Where each view is actually protected, since the two mechanisms are not interchangeable.**

| | Is the column in the frame? | What stops it becoming a feature |
|---|---|---|
| C1, C2 | no — censoring drops it | censoring, with the trainer's exclusion as backup |
| C3, C4 | **yes**, and it must be — it is the price head's target | **the trainer's exclusion alone** |

Censoring does nothing for C3 and C4 by design. So for exactly the two views where a leak would manufacture
the SSP result, `SETTLEMENT_COLS` is the only line of defence, and gate 3's visibility condition is what
catches the other direction — a wrong `SSP_ONLY_NODES` handing the column to C1 and C2 as well.

##### 8e. Metric names, and the one word that names two quantities

**`profit CPM` becomes `profit per 1,000 wins`.** CPM means per thousand IMPRESSIONS and every price column
is a CPM, but this figure divides by WINS, so the old label hid its own denominator and invited comparison
with `value_captured`, whose denominator is all rows. JSON key `profit_per_1k_wins`, computed once in
`metrics.economics` as `profit / wins * 1000`, nan when `wins == 0`. It stays in the no-claim set and carries
no verdict.

**`ev_spearman` leaves every generated document and stays in `results.json`.** Its removal was started and
left half-done: it was taken out of the dissertation outline and the results docx, and still appears in
`t9v2/docs/V2_Results.md` as "EV spearman" in the main table and the caveat line. So: no column in the
per-view table, no contrast rows, no scale-stability rows, but `ev.spearman` and `ev.spearman_active` remain
as stored diagnostics. A test asserts the literal string "spearman" appears nowhere in the generated v2.2
markdown, because a half-done removal is what produced this state.

**`ev_ratio` names two different quantities today, and the merged table's vocabulary wins.** They are not
variants of one measure; they answer different questions at different stages:

| | Formula | Question | Oracle reads |
|---|---|---|---|
| **`ev_ratio`**, the valuation LEVEL | `mean(predicted EV) / mean(true EV)` | is the view's price tag on an impression accurate, before any bidder touches it | exactly 1.0, by definition |
| **`value_captured`** | `value(won rows) / value(all rows)` | did the bidder actually win the valuable rows | 0.89 — even a perfect valuer cannot win everything |

The level isolates the MMP mechanism on its own: C1 and C3 learn the funnel from won rows only, a
value-selected sample, so they under-predict value everywhere and read below 1 whatever the bidder then does.
At 1M, C1 is 0.302 against C2's 0.853. Value captured is a bidder outcome and depends on the win curve, the
ladder and the argmax; the same pair reads 0.139 against 0.229.

The collision: `metrics.economics` returns VALUE CAPTURED under the JSON key `ev_ratio`, so
`stage6_aggregate.py` prints `ev_ratio` meaning captured while `merged_results_table.py` prints `ev_ratio`
meaning level and labels captured correctly. **The code's own comment settles which is intended** —
`bidders.ev_bias` records that `ratio` was named so it "cannot be mistaken for the value-capture ratio next to
it". The field name is the historical accident.

**Approved by Ken, 22 August 2026.** So the JSON key `economics.<policy>.ev_ratio` is renamed to `value_captured`. **This is a breaking change to
`results.json`**, so v2's thirty committed files use the old key and any tool reading both must know which
schema it holds; the design fingerprint already distinguishes them.

**Open: `RATIO_FLOOR`.** `stage6_aggregate.py` blanks a profit ratio whose base is below an absolute
1000. Nothing blanks today, because profits are still in eCPM-sums and clear it easily. But step 2's
units fix divides every profit by 1000, and C1's profit then reads 9.4 at 100K, 204 at 1M and 3,544 at
10M — so the 100K and 1M profit ratios silently go `n/a`, including the 1M headline. The fix is to make
the floor relative, one percent of that seed's own oracle profit, which cannot rot when units change.
Not yet approved.

##### 8f. What v2.2 publishes, and what stays frozen

**Ken, 22 August 2026: v2.2's numbers replace v2's headline wholesale, with v2 kept as a comparison row.**
Nothing is mixed. The floor fix moves C1 win AUC from 0.8720 to 0.8195, the units fix divides every profit by
1000, and the new ladder moves every argmax, so a v2 number set beside a v2.2 number is not a comparison of
data layers, it is a comparison of two different simulators.

| File | Fate |
|---|---|
| `t9v2/docs/V2.2_Results.md` | new — all 30 datasets, three scales |
| `t9v2/docs/V2.2_Results_10M_n10_CI.md` | new — the v1-layout tables at 10M |
| `t9v2/docs/V2_Results.md` | **byte-identical, never regenerated, never deleted** |
| `t9v2/docs/V2_Results_Merged_CI.md` | as above |

Dotted `v2.2`, matching the Specification and Plan filenames already in `docs/`. The writer raises if any
output basename equals a v2 filename, because the current writer overwrites its output unconditionally and v2
is published at tag `v2.0.0` — its numbers must stay quotable.

##### 8g. One reporting script, and the four it replaces

`stage6_aggregate.py`, `merged_results_table.py`, `results_1m.py` and `results_across_seeds.py` are replaced by
a single `t9v2/tools/results_report.py --scale {100K,1M,10M,all}`, and **the four are deleted rather than left
beside it**. Between them they currently hold four copies of the confidence-interval arithmetic, two meanings
of `ev_ratio` and two labels for profit-over-wins. Leaving them in place is what let those divergences appear
and would let them reappear.
