#### The bid ladder — SETTLED 22 August 2026

**`geomspace(0.1, 1200, 60)` in CPM, replacing `geomspace(0.1, 120, 48)`.** Shared by every policy:
the classifier bidder, the price bidder, `truth_ev` and the oracle.

**The ceiling was the defect, and it is far larger than the spacing.** Measured on seed 20250 at 100K
under the TRUE win rule, so the figures are pure grid effect with no model error in them. Loss is
against a near-continuous 4,000-rung reference over the same range.

| Grid | Loss |
|---|---:|
| `geomspace(0.1, 120, 48)` — the current ladder | **7.24%** |
| `geomspace(0.1, 1200, 48)` — same rungs, ceiling raised | 0.69% |
| `geomspace(0.3, 1200, 60)` — trimmed floor, **rejected**, see below | 0.53% |
| `geomspace(0.1, 1200, 60)` — **adopted** | **0.53%** |
| `geomspace(0.1, 1200, 96)` | 0.32% |

Our own bids top out at 26.4 and never approach the old ceiling, which is why it looked generous. The
market does not: `m^win` reaches 971 and `ev` reaches 16,148 CPM on whale traffic, so the top rung
binds on 0.76% of rows and about 20% of the market clears above the highest bid the ladder can
express. On those rows the argmax is clipped and the bidder cannot bid what it should — a
one-directional bias, unlike spacing, which is noise.

**Resolution is second-order and was the wrong thing to worry about.** Doubling 48 to 96 rungs at a
fixed range recovers 0.2 percentage points, because the profit function is flat at its own maximum:
an 8% error in the bid is a second-order error in profit. The ceiling is first-order.

**The floor stays at 0.1, and the first draft of this section got that wrong.** It proposed trimming to
0.3 on the ground that nothing clears below it, which is true by ROW COUNT and false by MONEY. Measured:
a 0.3 floor leaves **0.571%** of oracle profit sitting on the bottom rung against **0.039%** at 0.1.
That is the same error the quantile ladder makes two paragraphs below — counting rows where the
criterion is surplus — and it is recorded rather than quietly corrected because it was made twice in
one analysis. Sixty rungs over 0.1 to 1200 give a 16.9% step, marginally coarser than today's 16.3%,
which the resolution measurement above shows costs almost nothing; both boundaries are then clean.

**Constant ratio beats concentrating rungs where the bids are, and the margin is five-fold.** The
natural intuition is to put resolution where the price mass is, since two thirds of our bids fall
between 1 and 3. It is wrong. Holding the range fixed at 0.3-1200 and varying only the shape:

| Shape | Loss | rungs under \$1 | \$1-10 | over \$50 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| constant ratio | **0.53%** | 9 | 16 | 23 |
| quantiles of `m^win`, i.e. rungs where the bids are | 2.54% | 7 | 29 | 4 |
| quantiles of the surplus at stake | 0.84% | 3 | 25 | 13 |
| half and half | 0.67% | 6 | 20 | 18 |

**The criterion is where the money is, not where the bids are.** One row with `ev` near 400 clearing
at 90 carries more surplus than a hundred rows clearing at 2, and those rows live in the expensive
tail. A quantile ladder leaves four rungs above 50 to serve them and loses five times as much as
constant ratio, which allocates 23 rungs there simply by having equal ratios over a wide range.

Constant ratio has a second advantage that matters more for a rebuild: it needs two endpoints and a
count, where both quantile shapes need the true price distribution to construct. Nothing has to be
re-derived when the floor fix moves that distribution, and no ground-truth knowledge is baked into a
constant every policy shares.

**Coarseness does not distort the contrasts.** Tested directly, because that is the thing the study
reports. Two policies differing by 2% in price knowledge measure +0.14% apart on the 48-rung ladder,
+0.15% on the adopted one and +0.13% against a near-continuous grid. Rival bids are drawn from a
continuous lognormal rather than from a ladder, so a small edge moves a policy across rung boundaries
on a random subset of rows and averages in. Coarseness adds variance to a contrast, not bias. The
arms-race intuition — that real bidders tune bids finely — would transfer only if rivals also chose
from a grid, which they do not.

**One ladder for every policy, and this is a rule rather than a convenience.** Give the price head a
finer grid than the classifier and the two-bidder agreement rule collapses, because a disagreement
could no longer be attributed to the win curve rather than the grid. Give the oracle a finer grid and
`value_captured` absorbs a resolution gap that has nothing to do with information.

**Where it lands in the build order.** The ladder is a scoring setting in `training.yaml`
(`candidate_prices`), not a generator setting, so it invalidates trained results but NOT the master
parquets and forces no regeneration of its own. Adopt the shape at step 2, with the units fix, since
both are preconditions for quoting any economic number.

**The endpoints are a CHECKED PROPERTY, not a constant, and this is the point of the section.** The
measurements above are one seed at 100K on pre-floor-fix data, where floors run about 1.75 times
inflated and `m^win` with them, so 0.1 and 1200 cannot simply be carried forward. Rather than
re-guessing them by hand at step 5, they get a pass condition:

> **Boundary check.** Oracle profit earned on the TOP rung, and on the BOTTOM rung, must each stay
> below **0.1%** of total oracle profit. If either breaches, widen that end and re-score.

Measured today: the current ladder puts **1.528%** on the top rung, a clear breach and the defect
this section exists to fix. `geomspace(0.1, 1200, 60)` puts 0.000% on the top and 0.039% on the
bottom, so it passes with room.

**Profit at risk, not occupancy, is the measure.** Only 0.042% of ROWS sit on the current top rung,
which reads as negligible and is not: those rows carry 1.528% of the profit, because whale traffic is
rare and large. A row-count criterion would have declared the current ladder healthy.

This costs nothing to run — no regeneration, one scoring pass over one seed — and it makes step 5
mechanical: re-measure, widen whichever end breaches, record. The reason for a check rather than a
number is `floor_binds_rate`, four sections down: a hand-written constant that no code path measured,
which then drifted out of its own band with nothing able to notice.

**Not settled here.** Whether the boundary check should also govern the RUNG COUNT, by requiring that
halving the step change total oracle profit by less than some tolerance. Sixty is currently a judgement
rather than a solved number, though the resolution measurement above bounds what it can cost at about
0.2 percentage points.

### The price feature — Ken's position, 21 August 2026 — ⚠️ SUPERSEDED, kept as record

> **Read this as history, not as the design.** Its central argument — prefer the exact second-highest bid
> over the clipped `max(LU7, floor)` — was **REVERSED on 22 August 2026**. The quantity is
> `min_winning_price = max(LU7, floor)`, on every row. The reversal and its reasoning are in **build-order
> step 3**; the measured consequences are in **5a** and **5d**.
>
> It is kept rather than deleted because step 3 is a reversal, and a reversal is unreadable without the
> position it reverses. Where this section says "second-highest bid", the live name is `min_winning_price`.

**The quantity is the second-highest bid, not `min_bid_to_win`.** Ken settled this on 21 Aug and it
supersedes the July argument that dropped a second-highest-bid field as inapplicable to a first-price
market. That argument confused prominence with existence. Under first-price clearing the winner no
longer pays a cent above the runner-up, so the second-highest bid stops being the *clearing rule* —
but it still exists in every auction, and it is the quantity **bid shading** is guided by. Exchanges
return this feedback precisely because shading models need the runner-up distribution.

**Why it gives the full price picture.** In T9, `LU7` is the highest rival bid and
`won = bid ≥ max(LU7, floor)`. From the DSP's seat:

| Row class | What LU7 is | Status today |
|---|---|---|
| won | the **second-highest bid**, the runner-up that was beaten | not exposed |
| lost, sold | the **winning price** | already visible to C3/C4 |
| lost, unsold | unobserved, only `LU7 < floor` is known | censored |

Second-highest-on-won plus winning-price-on-lost therefore yields **LU7 observed on every sold row**.
That is what collapses the interval censoring into a point observation, and it is what makes
workstream 3, the move to plain regression, possible rather than cosmetic.

**Prefer it over `max(LU7, floor)`.** The clipped form loses information whenever the floor binds:
you learn only `LU7 ≤ floor`. As a regression target, exact beats clipped. This also supersedes v1's
arm **B1**, which used the clipped won-rows-only form.

**Carry this caveat.** v1 ran B1, the strongest won-row price feedback an exchange could offer, and it
did **not** move overpayment: −0.8% [−2.6, +1.0], paired across ten seeds
(`docs/KDD_Paper_Draft_v2.md:517`). v2.2's target is ranking rather than overpayment, and the construct
here is the more informative one, so the finding does not transfer directly. It is recorded because
the closest prior test came back empty.

### The anti-leak gate — the decision that decides whether any of this is valid — ⚠️ SETTLED, kept as record

> **Read this as the statement of the problem, not as an open question.** It was settled on 22 August 2026,
> and NOT as the new gate its title implies: the check is a **pass condition on gates 3 and 4**, per this
> section's own instruction that it needs "gate 3's equivalent, stated as a pass condition". Gate 3 gains the
> column's per-view visibility; gate 4 gains the fitted-feature check. **8d** carries the one test that
> survived, and 5c carries the `SSP_ONLY_NODES` edit this section's worry actually depends on.
>
> Its analysis of why the current row's LU7 must never reach the model is unchanged and still governs.

**Current row versus history is the whole question.** At bid time the bidder does not know this
auction's LU7. If the model is given it, `won = bid ≥ max(LU7, floor)` becomes near-deterministic and
the model has been handed its own label. That is not a subtle risk: it is exactly how v1's
`bid_density` leaked, and v1's own SHAP shows the model reached for it hard — **0.21 under C3, top-4
in 3 of 3 seeds** (`docs/SHAP_Analysis_v10.md:76,133`). A C3 gain produced that way is an artifact of
the design, not a property of SSP data, and v1's headline SSP claim died of it.

So the feature enters as **history** — lagged, aggregated, or per-cell — never as the current row's
value. The gate must prove that the current row's LU7 cannot reach the model in any view. Gate 3
already proves no latent is exposed; this needs its equivalent, stated as a pass condition and
reported per view.

**Two residuals to design around.** Unsold rows stay censored, `LU7 < floor`, so the regression runs
over sold rows and some censoring handling survives at that boundary. And the visibility rule needs
stating per row class in the Specification, not here.

### Open decisions — settle before building — ✅ ALL THREE ANSWERED, 22 August 2026

> | # | Decision | Where it was answered |
> |---:|---|---|
> | 1 | The exact historical form of the feature | **5d** — a fifth encoder over `min_winning_price`, shared cell key, leave-one-out mandatory |
> | 2 | How the sold/unsold boundary is handled | **step 6** — it disappears. `max(LU7, floor)` is defined on every row, so nothing is censored and unsold rows read the floor exactly |
> | 3 | Which numbers the dissertation cites | **8f** — v2.2 replaces v2's headline wholesale, v2 kept as a comparison row, nothing mixed (Ken, 22 Aug) |
>
> The table below is the original wording, kept because the reasons it gives for why each decision mattered
> are still the reasons the answers are what they are.

| # | Decision | Why it matters |
|---:|---|---|
| 1 | **The exact historical form** of the second-highest-bid feature: lagged per auction, per-cell aggregate, or an encoder over both | Decides whether the anti-leak gate can be stated as a hard rule or needs a statistical test |
| 2 | **How the sold/unsold boundary is handled** once LU7 is observed on sold rows | Determines whether workstream 3 is a clean switch to regression or a hybrid that keeps a censored tail |
| 3 | **Which numbers the dissertation cites**, v2.0 or v2.2 | The dissertation reports v2. If v2.2 moves a headline, §7 Results and the abstract move with it |

### Relationship to the post-submission design queue

The queue below (four items, plus the sigma item now held in the v2.1 addition file) predates this
scope and is not superseded by it. Item 1, the **encoder-key diagnostic**, is the one to run first:
it tests the same hypothesis as workstream 2 — that the SSP null is partly a representation failure —
but costs hours and needs no regeneration, whereas workstream 2 needs a schema change and invalidates
30 datasets. If the signal is already present and merely averaged away by the encoder key, the new
feature may be unnecessary.

Note also that the proposed feature is close kin to v1's arm **B1** (`min_bid_to_win`), abandoned
24 July 2026 — though for weaker reasons than the ones motivating it here.

### Queued tasks (v2.2's own queue)

*Distinct from the inherited post-submission design queue below, which is v2's.*

**Q1. Cite v1's `bid_density` SHAP weight as evidence that the leak was load-bearing.** v1's SHAP
analysis puts `bid_density` at **0.21 under C3, top-4 in 3 of 3 seeds**
(`docs/SHAP_Analysis_v10.md:76, 133`; the 10M rerun reproduced the tracked JSON bit-identically at
`bid_density 0.21176`). This matters twice over. For the write-up, it shows v1's leak was not a
marginal contaminant but one of the strongest features in its win model, which is why v1's SSP lift
was an artifact rather than a small bias. For v2.2, it is the concrete precedent behind open decision
3: a price feature close to the Tier-2 label will be reached for hard by the model, exactly as
`bid_density` was, so the anti-leak gate has to be designed on the assumption that it will be
exploited if it can be.

**Q2. Sweep the ROAS target, and report `placed_rate` beside profit.** The gate shipped at target 1
(`e7c7830`) and the target has never been varied. Sweeping it is the natural future test and costs
nothing to run: the gate is a **scoring-side** change, so a sweep runs over existing masters and frozen
bundles with no regeneration and no refit, and it rides along free with any batch.

*What the sweep is for.* Target 1 is break-even, so it only declines rows that would have lost money.
A target above 1 declines rows that were profitable but thin, trading volume for margin, and the
question is whether the C2−C1 and C3−C1 contrasts hold their shape as margin tightens. A layer worth
having when the buyer is indiscriminate is not obviously worth the same to a buyer with a return
floor, and no result in this study currently speaks to that. It is the closest thing v2.2 has to
**RQ4** — under what market conditions price data helps — on the demand side rather than the supply
side.

*Why it is not free of design questions, and they are open.* Three, in the order they bite.

- **What the sweep is scored against.** At target 1 the learned bidder places every row and the
  true-value policies place 0.2620, so `value_vs_oracle` already divides two policies gated to very
  different degrees. Raising the target moves the numerator and not the denominator, and whether the
  oracle should be swept alongside or held at 1 as a fixed ceiling is undecided. Holding it fixed keeps
  one reference point across the sweep; sweeping it keeps the comparison like-for-like at each target.
- **Where the gate stops being inert.** The learned head cannot predict an exact zero, so the gate does
  nothing to it at target 1. Somewhere above 1 it starts to bite, and that threshold is a property of
  the head's predicted-value distribution rather than of the market. It should be measured before the
  sweep grid is chosen, or the grid will be mostly no-ops and then a cliff.
- **Whether calibration follows.** Calibration at the recommended bid is already scored on placed rows
  only, so its row set shrinks as the target rises and `ece_at_recommended` becomes a number over a
  progressively more selected subpopulation. Comparable across views at one target, not obviously
  comparable across targets.

*Not started, and it is not a v2.2 deliverable.* Recorded here so the gate is not left as a switch
nobody ever moved.

**Q3. Replace σ ≈ 0.9 with a better-justified value.** Ken, 23 August 2026: keep option B and keep σ at about
0.9 **as a temporary value**. The procedure — read the scale off C3's residuals — is what was decided; the
number is what it currently returns, 0.9024 at 100K and 0.8911 at 1M.

*Why it is queued rather than settled.* The value is defensible and it is not optimal. C1's own accuracy
optimum is near 0.50, and the gap between 0.50 and 0.90 is worth about 0.26 of C1's rmse_log and roughly four
times the reported price contrast. Neither of the two legitimate alternatives beats it: minimising C1's error
against `m^win` needs the answer C1 never sees, and C1's own censored likelihood picks 0.44, which is measurably
worse. So there is no better answer available today, only a known cost.

*What would actually settle it.* A criterion that identifies the AFT scale from interval data without using
`m^win`. The obstacle is real and may not be removable — 70 percent of C1's rows are right-censored and carry
almost no information about scale — so the honest outcome may be that σ stays borrowed and the limitation
stands. Until then step 8 reports the contrast at the derived σ **beside its floor**, so the cost is visible
rather than absorbed.

*Not on the critical path.* v2.2 ships with the temporary value.

### Not decided here

The schema, the node definitions and the generator laws are the Specification's business, not this
document's. This section records scope only.

   > evaluator assumed, and v2 does not do this because its oracle rides the exact step of a first-price
   > auction rather than the AFT curve. What is unanswered is the value. Sigma sets the width of the win
   > curve, the width sets the chosen bid, and the bid sets every economic number the AFT bidder reports,
   > so an unjustified constant sits directly on the C3 minus C1 contrast. Fitting it per view would be
   > worse, putting a free parameter on the same contrast. Scoring side only, no regeneration, runs over
   > existing data and trained models.

**Two problems described here are real, whatever the standing of the document that raised them.**
They are recorded as candidates, not as decisions:

- **The sigma question is unresolved and it sits on the SSP result.** v2.2's workstream 3 moves from
  survival regression to plain regression, which may dissolve the question rather than answer it. If
  any survival component survives, sigma still needs a justified value, and "copied from v1" is not one.
- **The one-Tier-2-head decision was reversed without being written up.** v2's plan says one Tier-2
  head; the second bidder gave it two. v2.2 carries two heads by design, so the reversal belongs in the
  plan rather than sitting implicit in the code.

**A defect to avoid repeating.** v2.1 labelled its design units `D1` and `D5`. That collides with the
Specification's `D` column family, where `D1`–`D4` are the time columns (timestamp, hour_of_day,
day_of_week, week) — two meanings for one label across the document set. If the change-log pattern is
re-adopted, number the design units `U1…Un`.

---


## Post-submission design queue (added 18 Aug 2026)

*Four decisions from the 18 Aug design discussions, parked here until after the dissertation
submission. Ordered by the agreed sequence, cheapest diagnostic first.*

**1. Encoder-key diagnostic. Run this first, it costs hours and no regeneration.** The SSP price
history reaches the win model as shrunken cell means keyed by (app_id, slot_format, ad_exchange,
daypart). The rival private structure varies along two axes that key does not contain, LR2 by
(os x device) segment and LR3 by day. Whatever signal the private structure puts into prices
along those axes is averaged away before the model sees it. Test whether the SSP null is partly
a representation failure by adding segment and day to the encoder key on the existing datasets.
The outcome tells us what the LR dials should even be set to, so it gates item 3.

**2. Auction ID into the node register.** Schema change, new design fingerprint, invalidates all
30 datasets. Rides in the same regeneration batch as item 3.

**3. LR1-6 retune for C3/C4.** Tune the rival-pool latents that only the SSP views can learn
about, informed by item 1. Settings change, so regeneration.

**4. ROAS-target bidder.** A fourth policy beside learned, truth_ev and oracle. Scoring side
only, runs over existing data and trained models, no regeneration. Rides along free with any
batch. Chosen over a budget-constrained buyer (Ken, 18 Aug).

**Sequencing.** Item 1 first. Then one batched regeneration carrying items 2 and 3 together,
with item 4 alongside. Re-running stages 1-7 as a single better-shipped product is agreed in
principle, on Ken's condition, only if we are sure the decisions make sense. Nothing here starts
before the dissertation is submitted.

## 2. What gets built

*In brief.* One installable Python package, `t9v2`, in its own folder under Python 3.13. Everything that can change a result lives in 7 settings files rather than in code, so the whole thing runs without editing anything. The 78 generator variables are entries in those files, one law each. The subsections below take it in pipeline order, from the settings through generation, censoring, training and scoring.

### The 6 functions and 3 commands

3 console commands. `t9v2-generate`, `t9v2-run` and `t9v2-campaign`. They sit over 6 public functions. `t9v2-run` calls `evaluate`, and `t9v2-campaign --aggregate-only` calls `aggregate`. Each function is described below.

1. `generate(profile, scale, seed)` writes the master parquet.
2. `censor(master, view)` returns one of the 4 views.
3. `train(view)` fits the model stack on that view.
4. `evaluate(profile, scale, seed)` runs one seed end to end.
5. `predict(view, row) -> ev, pwin` scores a single row.
6. `aggregate(profile, scale)` builds the results table from the per-seed files.

### Settings, the 7 files and how they merge

A profile is a named block of settings. Everything that can change a result has one home. Settings merge key by key, the 5 domain files first, then the chosen `profiles.yaml` block, then the checksummed `calibrated.yaml`. 7 files.

**Where these came from.** v1 had 6 settings files and only 3 of the names carry over.

| v1 | v2 | What moved |
|---|---|---|
| `benchmarks.yaml` | `market.yaml` | The rival-pool bounds, the eCPM targets, the share vectors. Rho does not come here, it goes to `profiles.yaml` (open item O3 3d). The edge switches do not carry over |
| `benchmarks.yaml` | `training.yaml` | The historical-price switch, the encoder constants, the spend model's scale, the candidate price list, XGBoost parameters, split days |
| `archetypes.yaml` | `graph.yaml` + `tables.yaml` | The 5 archetypes become rows in the network. Their Beta and LogNormal parameters become law parameters, their shares become a table |
| `bn_cpts.yaml` | `tables.yaml` | The 6 live probability tables, plus the 3 dead ones, wired by open item O1 on 15 August 2026. `tables.yaml` carries 9 |
| — | `graph.yaml` | New. The 78 variables with their parents, laws, streams and observability. Nothing in v1 corresponds |
| `profiles.yaml` | `profiles.yaml` | Same job, the override layer |
| `validation.yaml` | `validation.yaml` | Same job, plus `repro_tolerance` |
| `calibrated.yaml` | `calibrated.yaml` | Same job, machine-written |

`benchmarks.yaml` splits because one file served two consumers, so v1's scoring stack cannot load without the generator's settings. Separating them is what lets `predict` lift into a bidder later. `archetypes.yaml` disappears because archetypes are 5 rows of the network like any other variable, and giving them their own file kept their parameters apart from every other law.

**The 7 files.**

| File | What it holds | Why it is separate |
|---|---|---|
| `graph.yaml` | the 78 built rows, their laws, parents, streams and observability | the structure of the network |
| `tables.yaml` | the 9 probability tables | keeps bulky numeric blocks out of the structure |
| `market.yaml` | the rival sampling bounds and the rest of the generator constants, each with value, route and source. Not rho, which lives in the profile | consumed by the generator half only |
| `training.yaml` | the `hist_winning_price` switch, the encoders' single shared shrinkage constant (open item O13), the spend model's scale, the candidate price list, XGBoost parameters, split days, the calibration measures, and the attribution sample count and seed | consumed by the scoring half only, which can then load without the generator |
| `validation.yaml` | the calibration targets, the direction checks and `repro_tolerance` | the pass criteria must not sit with the values they judge |
| `profiles.yaml` | the override layer. Each profile states only the values it changes | one place to see what a run changed |
| `calibrated.yaml` | the solved constants, machine-written with a checksum | never hand-edited |

Rho is how strongly rival bidders' valuations move together, 0 independent and 1 identical. It has one home and that home is the profile, since it is a property of a run rather than of the design (open item O3 3d). A direction check asserts that an effect points the way the design says, for example that a higher bid wins more often. Seeds are one list per profile, the rest derived by index.

The `default` block holds rho and names the `hist_winning_price` override, the 10 seeds 20250 to 20259, and the 3 campaign scales plus a `golden_test` scale at 200,000 rows for fingerprint tests. There are no edge switches. The 6 dependencies, being pairing, exposure, os_spend, payer_timing, hour and `rival_pool`, are always wired, so they are properties of the design rather than settings. Open item O11 records that decision.

### The generator and the 78 variables

Every generator variable is one entry in `config/graph.yaml`, built from the node register. `config/tables.yaml` holds the 9 probability tables.

A plate is how often a variable is drawn. The 6 plates are per user, per app, per campaign, per advertiser, per rival and per auction. A plate value is held constant across every row that entity appears in.

Each entry declares the fields below.

| Field | Values |
|---|---|
| `plate` | one of the 6 above |
| `parents` | the variables its law reads |
| `edge_group` | the name of the one random-number stream it draws from |
| `columns` | the parquet columns it emits, or none |
| `type` | its value type and limits |
| `law` | the rule turning parents into a value, one of the 4 types below |
| `kind` | `column`, written to the parquet. `internal`, never written. `pool`, a frozen object rather than a table row |
| `observability` | the censoring map as data. `latent`, `all`, or a per-view map over C1 to C4 with row rules `all`, `won`, `sold`, `none` |

**The 4 types.** Every variable is produced by exactly one of these. The specification defines them formally and states what test each must pass.

| Type | What it does | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **T1** calibrated draw | One draw from a fixed table or distribution. Nothing feeds it | which archetype a user is, 2% whale and so on |
| **T2** probability table | A draw from a table, with the parents choosing the row | hour of day, drawn from a table that depends on the archetype |
| **T3** conditional distribution | A draw whose settings come from its parents | spend, where the archetype decides the mean |
| **T4** deterministic formula | A calculation with no randomness at all. Also covers summarising many values into one, and rules that pick which rows something applies to | expected value, the funnel numbers multiplied together. Or the highest of the 8 rival bids |

Two rules go with them. A deterministic law names a function that already exists in the code, so a settings file never holds a formula as text that gets run. And where a variable is switched off for some rows, the draw still happens and the value is then set to zero, which is what keeps the random numbers lined up.

**Random numbers.** Each variable draws from its own named stream, seeded from the run's seed plus a hash of the stream's name. Because the streams are named rather than numbered in order, adding or reordering a variable does not shift the numbers every other variable receives.

Auction rows are drawn in fixed blocks of 65,536, with a fresh generator per block. That block size is a lineage constant, never a setting, which is what makes the same seed produce the same data whatever chunk size the file is written in. Rival pacing is indexed by the absolute calendar day rather than the row's position in the file.

**The variables.** 78 active variables in one network, sampled in a fixed order, each with exactly one law. 30 of them emit no column and the other 48 emit 55 between them. No rows are declared absent. Open item O1 wired the last 3 probability tables, so `tables.yaml` carries all 9.

The bidder's value estimate `eltv_b2` is deliberately not the truth, and the ablation measures how much of that gap each data layer closes.

### The 11 startup checks

V1 to V11 run when the settings are read, before any data is made. Each stops the run with an error naming the variable, the file and the key.

1. **V1.** Graph acyclicity and parent existence.
2. **V2.** One entry per variable, with none unused.
3. **V3.** Every deterministic law names a function that exists.
4. **V4.** The `default` profile emits exactly the frozen 55 columns.
5. **V5.** Every declared parent is read by its own law.
6. **V6.** Every named table exists in `tables.yaml`. A conditional table sums to 1 per row. A joint table sums to 1 over all cells. `graph.yaml` declares which kind each table is.
7. **V7.** Every settings path resolves.
8. **V8.** `edge_group` is one of the stream groups declared in `graph.yaml`, and the declared set is closed.
9. **V9.** Stream names are declared once and never positional.
10. **V10.** `observability` covers 4 views with a legal row rule.
11. **V11.** No setting resolves twice at the same layer.

V3 needs the generator's named functions, so it is built in stage 2 and the other 10 in stage 1. V4's column list comes from the specification and the node register, not from v1's code.

### Censoring into the 4 views

The operator is censoring and the object it returns is a view. The `observability` field in `graph.yaml` declares each view's column rules and row rules, so a view is read out of the settings rather than written in code. Views are applied in memory at training time and never written during the campaign.

From one truth-retained auction stream, censoring produces 4 views that differ only in observability, which data layers are visible.

1. **C1, DSP-only.** The buyer's own bid logs, with the funnel on won rows only.
2. **C2, DSP+MMP.** Adds the funnel, click, install, payer and spend, on every row rather than won rows only.
3. **C3, DSP+SSP.** Adds the price and competition columns.
4. **C4, integrated.** All 3 data layers.

### Training in 8 modules

1. `features.py`, per-view column selection.
2. `encoder.py`, the 2 historical winning price encoders. A DSP encoder fitted on won-row own bids and served to all 4 views, and an SSP encoder fitted on winning prices and served to C3 and C4 only.
3. `tier1.py`, the 4 stacked models. Click, install given click, payer given install, and spend given payer, each trained on the rows that passed the step before.
4. `tier2.py`, **one head**, a binary classifier of win given bid. v1 also ran an AFT survival model of the competing bid; v2 does not. See below for what that costs and why it is affordable.
5. `bidders.py`, the profit-max, incumbent and oracle bidders registered by name.
6. `metrics.py`.
7. `runner.py`, one view end to end.
8. `shap_report.py`, per-feature attribution of one prediction, off by default.

Fitting is separated from scoring in both tiers. Every model writes a manifest naming its features in order, its encodings, its price units in dollars per impression, its view, its profile, its seed and its revision.

**Why Tier-2 has one head, and what that costs.** Ken's decision, 15 August 2026. v1 ran 2 heads, an
AFT survival model of the competing bid and a classifier of win given bid. v2 keeps only the classifier.

**Why the classifier.** It assumes nothing about the shape of the price distribution. The AFT head does,
and when that assumption is wrong the error does not stay in the price model, it flows into the win
curve, into the chosen bid, and out as a money number. In v1 that is exactly what happened: the AFT
bidder showed an SSP overpayment reduction that the classifier showed to be about zero. The classifier
was right, so v2 keeps the head that was right.

**What is given up.** 4 metrics, all of which need a predicted price that a classifier does not have:
`price_rmse_all`, `price_rmse_lost`, `price_crps_all` and `price_crps_lost`. The lost-row slice is the
real loss, since scoring a predicted price on rows whose price was never observed is the most direct
measurement of the censoring story. v2 measures SSP value through win AUC and profit instead, which is
narrower but sound, and the limitation is declared rather than discovered.

**What is not given up.** `ece_win` and `mce_win`. Those are calibration measures on a win probability,
the classifier has one, and v1 simply never computed them for it, giving it logloss instead. Ken's same
decision adds both. With 2 heads they were never scored on a common footing; with one that asymmetry
disappears.

**Why this costs nothing the plan had asked for.** Overpay is already not a v2 metric, so the
AFT-versus-classifier comparison had no v2 consumer. And none of the scored figures below is a price
metric, so no planned output depended on the head being dropped.

**If an AFT head is ever restored**, its sigma question has to be settled first. v1's single `AFT_SCALE`
trained the model, shaped its win curve, scored its CRPS **and** built the oracle ceiling every view was
judged against, so the fitted model was handed the same sigma the evaluator assumed. That is not open
item O12, which is `spend_model.scale` on the Tier-1 spend head, a different parameter with no v1
counterpart at all. The 2 were briefly conflated on 15 August and are kept apart here deliberately.

### Scoring, the metrics and the bidders

`evaluate` calls `generate`, `censor` and `train` in turn, generating the master, censoring it into all 4 views, training the stack on each, then scoring them against the retained truth. It is not a peer of the other functions, it wraps them, and it is what the campaign calls 30 times. `generate`, `censor` and `train` are called directly only to work on a stage in isolation.

Scoring runs inside `evaluate`, once per seed, over all 4 views. 8 figures are computed.

1. Click AUC.
2. Install AUC.
3. Payer AUC.
4. Win AUC.
5. Spend CRPS.
6. Profit, and `ev_ratio`, the share of true expected value a view recovers.
7. ECE, expected calibration error, for the 4 probability heads, click, install, payer and win. The average gap between predicted probability and observed frequency.
8. MCE, maximum calibration error, for the same 4 heads. The largest single-bin gap, so a head with a small ECE but one badly wrong region is still caught. Both are measured and reported per head per view, never fitted, per open item O7. Adding them to the win head is Ken's decision of 15 August, closing an asymmetry in v1, which reported calibration for its AFT head only and gave the classifier logloss instead.

Stage 4 builds the bidders, the metrics and the economics together, so the money is computed on the same seed in the same call as the ranking metrics. 3 bidders are registered in `bidders.py` by name.

| Bidder | What it reads | Served |
|---|---|---|
| profit-max | `ev` and the `pwin` curve at each candidate price | yes |
| incumbent | the same, under the reference rule | yes |
| oracle | the retained truth, so it is the ceiling rather than a learned bidder | never, which the serving whitelist enforces |

Only the averaging is deferred to aggregation.

**Also at stage 4: the archetype tilt sweep.** The 3 tilt strengths set at open item O3 3b are the
only invented numbers in the build that no gate can catch. The rake preserves each table's marginal
whatever tau is, so 0.13 and 0.26 both pass every check identically. The sweep is the substitute for a
gate.

It runs here rather than at stage 6 because stage 5 spends the campaign. A sweep that runs afterwards
can only tell you the 30 datasets were built on a value that mattered; a sweep that runs before can
still change the decision.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Arms** | tau x {0, 0.5, 1, 2}, from `tables.yaml` `meta.tilt_sensitivity_sweep`, so the shipped values 0.13 / 0.13 / 0.04 become 0 / half / shipped / double |
| **Scale** | 100K, 3 seeds per arm, 12 runs. The rho sweep used the same shape. Read the trend, not the levels: 100K levels are efficiency-inflated |
| **Paired** | the SAME 3 seeds in every arm. The effect is small, and different seeds per arm would let seed noise swamp it |
| **Measured** | C3 minus C1 win AUC, C2 minus C1 install and payer AUC, and profit. One row per arm |
| **Passes when** | the contrasts stay inside their intervals across the 4 arms, which says the result does not rest on the invented value |

**What a failure means.** If a contrast does move with tau, the sweep has not failed, it has found
something: a headline that depends on a number nobody can source. That is reported as a limitation.
The one thing that must not happen is running it and not reporting it.

**Also at stage 4: the private-amplitude experiment, tried and REVERTED (16 Aug 2026).** The SSP
result rests on how much of the clearing price is private rather than public. At the shipped setting
`private_share_of_log_lu7` is 0.178, so the price is 82 percent public, which is why a lone DSP
reaches 0.87 win AUC from its own bid and the floor alone and why the SSP layer has little left to
explain. The obvious question is whether SSP is null only because that share is low, so the amplitude
was raised to find out.

Tripling `beta_R` and `w_k` did exactly what it was meant to do on the identification side: the
private share reached 0.44 and C1's win AUC fell to 0.798, opening the gap SSP would have to fill.
It was reverted anyway, because the same change broke the economics. Rival bids scale as
`exp(1.8 z)`, which is 36x at z = 2, so the highest-value rows became unwinnable at any profitable
price. C2's profit went negative and the ORACLE's own capture fell from 0.90 to 0.52 — the ceiling
itself collapsed, which means the market had stopped being one any bidder could operate in.

**The finding is a bound, not a null result.** The private amplitude has an economic ceiling well
below 3x. Identification and profitability pull in opposite directions here, and the shipped 0.178
sits where both are viable. Raising it to rescue the SSP contrast would buy a stronger result in a
market that no longer resembles the one being modelled, which is why this is recorded rather than
retried.

The full record lives with the target it constrains, `config/validation.yaml` on
`private_share_of_log_lu7`, so it cannot drift from the number it justifies.

**The tau = 0 arm does a second job.** `tables.yaml` claims tau = 0 reproduces a parentless draw
exactly. Compare that arm's fingerprint against a run with the 3 tilt tables removed entirely. They
must match bit for bit. If they do not, the dial is not wired as specified, which is a build defect
and is separate from whether tau matters.

**Carried into stage 4: one open decision and one trap.** After the gate-1 provenance sweep, exactly one
settings value in the whole build still has no source, and it lands here.

- **`spend_model.scale` is the only remaining hole**, and closing it is a design decision rather than a
  search. Decide first whether the parameter exists: v1's spend head is a plain regression scored on
  `rmse`, which has no scale, so the key may have been written for something the design does not have.
  Delete it if head 4 stays a plain regression. Keep it and **fit** it if head 4 becomes distributional.
  Full statement at specification open item **O12**.
  **This plan already leans the second way.** Figure 5 above is **spend CRPS**, and CRPS needs a
  predictive distribution, which a plain regression does not give. v1 never hit this because v1 reported
  only `rmse_spend`, a point metric. So either head 4 becomes distributional and the scale is fitted, or
  spend CRPS comes off the scored figures. That is a decision about this plan, not about a settings file.
  **Note this is a different question from the Tier-2 head Ken dropped on 15 August.** That decision was
  about the win model, where the choice was between an AFT price model and a classifier. This one is
  about the Tier-1 **spend** head, where the choice is between a plain regression and a censoring-aware
  model of spend. Dropping the Tier-2 AFT head does not answer it and does not close O12.
- **The trap.** v1's `AFT_SCALE = 1.0` looks like the answer and is not. It is the sigma of the
  **evaluator's** win curve, and it sets the oracle ceiling every view is scored against. Filling
  `spend_model.scale` with 1.0 by analogy would silently tie a model parameter to an evaluation
  parameter. While here, also settle why the generator's bid dispersion is 0.30 and the evaluator's win
  curve is 1.0, since both are a sigma on the same log-bid scale.

### Aggregation

`aggregate(profile, scale)` reads the per-seed result files for that scale and writes the means, the 95% intervals and the C2 minus C1 and C3 minus C1 contrasts. It opens no parquet and trains nothing, so it re-runs in minutes over data already produced. It runs once per scale at the end of the campaign, so 3 runs cover all 30 datasets, and again on its own after a seed is added or a metric is corrected.

### Predict, the single-row contract

`predict(view, row) -> ev, pwin` takes one row and returns 2 numbers. `ev` is the expected value of that impression and `pwin` is the chance of winning the auction for it. Batch scoring is vectorised, and `predict` is a single-row wrapper over the same model and the same feature order. Section 8's bidder plug-in point consumes `ev` and a `pwin` curve, so this contract is what lifts the scoring half into a bidder.

### Where it lives, the environment and the import test

v2 sits in `t9v2/`, on branch `t9-v2-rebuild`, cut from `t9-v11-mbw`. 

Python 3.13.7 is the only interpreter and every command uses it. A fresh `venv` under `t9v2/` holds the package editable. Its distribution and import name is `t9v2`, not `t9sim`, so a static check can tell a v1 import from a v2 import by name alone. v1 is never installed into it. Each seed writes one folder of parquet files. One seed end to end runs from that venv.

Stage 1 pins every dependency exactly, transitive packages included. shap is used only by the optional attribution report. The sampler is written by hand, with no third-party Bayesian network library.

The import test is 1 assertion. No `.py` file under `t9v2/` imports `t9sim`. It parses the import statements rather than searching the text, and fails naming the file and the line.

It cannot catch code copied across with the imports rewritten. The `SPEC_GAPS.md` log and the stage gates cover that case.

v2 writes its own tests. Settings and loader tests in stage 1, generator invariants in stage 2, the censoring tests in stage 3, and the leak and end-to-end tests in stage 4.

---

## 3. The stages

*In brief.* 7 stages in order, then the campaign the last 2 of them run. Each one ends with one artifact, and each artifact has a stated pass test. A stage begins only after the previous gate is approved. Gate 5 is the exception. It is a launch gate placed inside stage 5, written from campaign steps 1 to 3, with the unattended 10M seeds running after it is approved. Ken is the only reviewer and approval is Ken saying so, in any words. No bugs are planted for Ken to find. Every defect reported is real.

**Why gate 4's click-AUC floor is judged at 1M and not at 100K.** The floor was first written against the 100K seed, which was the wrong scale to put it at, and it was corrected to 1M (Ken, and restated 17 Aug 2026).

**The reason is the censoring, and it is structural rather than a matter of one seed being unlucky.** C1 and C3 see funnel labels on WON ROWS ONLY, so their click head trains on about 22,000 selected rows out of a 100K master, carrying a few hundred clicks. That cannot support per-app and per-campaign effects across hundreds of levels. C2 and C4, which see every row, reach 0.6531 and 0.6434 at the same scale. So at 100K the floor separates the censored views from the uncensored ones and nothing else: it re-measures the censoring, which the ablation already measures on purpose, rather than measuring whether the model works. At 1M the same views clear it with no change to the model, C1 at 0.5706 and C3 at 0.5731.

**Install AUC already had exactly this treatment**, in the row directly below: reported and not gated in C1 and C3, for the same reason at the same scale. Judging click AUC at 1M makes the two rows consistent instead of holding one of them to a threshold its own view cannot reach for a reason the design intends.

**The 100K numbers are still reported.** C1 0.5414 and C3 0.5435 appear in the gate 4 artifact and are below 0.55. They are reported and not gated, which is what the corrected rule says to do with them.

How a gate works. A gate 6 failure means a seed is missing or untrained, so those seeds go back to the campaign and are re-run until all 30 pass. Stage 7 does not start until gate 6 reads pass. Nothing in section 5's protected table is ever written to, and v2 writes only under `t9v2/output/` on seeds 20250 to 20259, so a v2 seed can never be mistaken for a deposit seed.

### Running the campaign, stages 5 and 6

30 datasets, 10 seeds each at 100K, 1M and 10M. Every one is generated, censored into 4 views, trained, evaluated and aggregated with confidence intervals. Steps 1 to 4 below are stage 5, steps 5 and 6 are stage 6.

**The count rule.** 30 datasets. Nothing is dropped. A dataset counts as done when it is generated, trained and evaluated.

**The seed list never changes.** Seeds 20250 to 20259 are fixed before the campaign starts. Generation is deterministic, so re-running a seed gives byte-identical data, and swapping in a different seed until a check passes would be selecting on the outcome.

**If a direction check fails**, count how many of the 10 seeds fail it. Most or all failing means a bug or an effect that is not there, so it is fixed and all 30 are regenerated. Exactly 1 failing is sampling noise on a weak effect, so the same check is read at 1M and 10M. If it holds there, it is reported and not gated at 100K, the same treatment install AUC already gets in C1 and C3.

**Timings.** On v1's measurements a seed takes about 25 seconds at 100K, 3.5 minutes at 1M and 42 minutes at 10M, which puts the whole campaign near 8 hours, and v2 replaces each estimate with its own first measurement at that scale.

### The order it runs in

+-----+--------------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------+
| #   | What runs                                              | Attended                       |
+=====+========================================================+================================+
| 1   | -   The 10 100K seeds                                  | yes                            |
+-----+--------------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------+
| 2   | -   The 10 1M seeds                                    | yes                            |
+-----+--------------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------+
| 3   | -   One watched 10M seed                               | yes                            |
|     | -   Gate 5 is written from steps 1 to 3                |                                |
+-----+--------------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------+
| 4   | -   The remaining 9 10M seeds                          | no, and it does not start      |
|     |                                                        | until gate 5 is approved       |
+-----+--------------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------+
| 5   | -   Aggregation across all 30                          | —                              |
+-----+--------------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------+
| 6   | -   One SHAP run at 1M                                 | —                              |
+-----+--------------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------+

If any attended run is not clean, gate 5 fails and the unattended run does not start.

### What makes the unattended run safe

+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------+
| Guard                      | What it does                                                 |
+============================+==============================================================+
| Fresh process per seed     | -   memory does not build up on a 16 GB laptop               |
+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------+
| Skip completed seeds       | -   a seed counts as complete only when `results.json`,      |
|                            |     written by `evaluate`, is present, parses and holds all  |
|                            |     4 views                                                  |
|                            | -   generation output alone is not enough, so a seed killed  |
|                            |     during training is re-run rather than skipped            |
|                            | -   `--force` re-runs a seed that is already complete        |
+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------+
| Disk guard                 | -   the driver will not start a seed without enough free     |
|                            |     space                                                    |
+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------+
| `keepawake.ps1`            | -   stops the machine sleeping                               |
+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------+
| Logging                    | -   all output is written to a log                           |
+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------+

Stage 5 builds the skip and the disk guard into v2's full-loop driver, and gate 5's kill-and-resume test proves them. Parquets are never auto-deleted.

## 4. What v2 takes from v1, and what it must never touch

*In brief.* v2 takes 3 things from v1, none of them code. It takes no code. Nothing already published is ever edited. A separate folder, a separate Python environment and a test that forbids importing v1's package keep the two apart.

### Never touched

v2 is allowed to disagree with v1 on everything it produces, its data, its results, its economics, even its headline conclusion. What it may never do is change something already published or already frozen.

Nothing in this table is modified, replaced, rewritten or deleted.

| Artifact | Where |
|---|---|
| Zenodo deposit | reserved DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21533031, not yet published. 14 files, 17.61 GB |
| Release repo tag | `v1.0.1` in github.com/QUMLKY/T9-simulator, private, mirrored at `release/public_repo/T9-simulator/`. The only `v1.0.1` anywhere, since this repository's duplicate was deleted on 14 August 2026 |
| v1 golden fingerprint | `0xdf0ac3e18624cf2b` |
| Result documents | `docs/v1/v10_Training_Results.md`, `docs/Method_Benchmark_10M_Results_13Jul2026.md`, the submitted paper |
| v1 environment and parquets | `t9_sim/venv`, the frozen v1 working tree, and `t9_sim/output/` for seeds 90213 to 90222 |

### The datasheet

A datasheet is the document that ships beside a dataset saying what it is and what it cannot be used for. v2 writes its own at stage 7.

It must carry every value whose route is `inferred`, because an inferred value is one no outside source backs. The provenance sweep leaves **108 of the 156 YAML leaves**, meaning terminal settings in the config tree rather than childless nodes in the DAG, on that route, so the list is long rather than short, and three entries are already named. (This sentence read "47 of the 83" until stage 7; the settings grew as stages 2 to 4 added laws. The datasheet is generated from the live settings rather than from this number, so it was never wrong — but the number here was.) The operating-system, version and device-type shares were never checked against an outside source and iPinYou cannot supply them, being desktop web traffic against a mobile-gaming market (open item O3 3a). Any archetype tilt strength chosen under O3 3b is likewise a design choice, not a measurement. And `ltv.base_median_usd`, the $6 median payer spend, was relabelled from `quoted` to `inferred` on 15 August because the project's own source register carries no such figure for the firms v1 cited.

### What carries over

2 things, and neither is code.

| What | Why it is copied rather than rebuilt |
|---|---|
| 6 calibration files | they cannot be recreated on this machine, and they are copied with their checksums |
| The design documents | they are what v2 is built from, and they carry every constant with its source |

v2 re-solves the calibration targets rather than importing v1's solved answers.

**The design documents.** Five of them, plus one that is deliberately excluded.

| Document | Role |
|---|---|
| `docs/T9Sim_Specification_v2.md` | the specification v2 is built from |
| `docs/T9Sim_Symbol_Plan.md` | the authority on notation |
| `docs/T9Sim_DGP_Node_Register.md` | one row per variable |
| `docs/v1/Known_Defects_Register.md` | v1's problem list, so v2 avoids repeating them |
| `docs/KDD_Terminology.md` | binds v2's variable names, view labels and prose |
| `docs/v1/T9Sim_Specification_v10.md` | the v1 record. **Not** a build input |

These documents are also where v2's numbers come from. The node register carries each constant next to the source it came from, so the probability tables, the operating-system and device shares, `shade`, `sigma_explore`, the spend decay factors and the archetype and category shares are all read from the documents rather than from v1's settings files.

v2 copies no value from v1's settings files unattributed. Stage 1 builds the 7 files from the documents and the conformance check reports every constant that arrived without a source. The gate-1 provenance sweep of 15 August traced all 25 of them and Ken adopted the provenance, so a value whose only surviving record is v1's own settings or code carries that file and line as its `source` rather than arriving bare. One hole is left, `spend_model.scale`, and it is decided at stage 4 as open item O12.

### When v2 may read v1's code

v2 is built from the documents. Reading v1's code is the exception, not the method, and it happens only when the documents do not answer the question.

This is the same rule as the settings rule above, applied to a different kind of answer. Code answers how a mechanism works, which is knowledge the documents can absorb. A settings value answers what a number is, so when v1 is its only surviving record the number is carried with that file and line as its source, which is what keeps it out of the hole list.

Every reading is logged in `t9v2/docs/SPEC_GAPS.md`. That log is the list of gaps in the specification and is delivered at gate 7. A gap that changes a design answer also adds a row to the open items.

### Keeping the two apart

Three things separate them. A separate folder, a separate Python environment, and the import test in section 2, which fails the build if any v2 import names v1's package.

Two v1 files are copied into `t9v2/` at stage 1, the script that holds the machine awake during the unattended run and the one that produces the Word copies of these documents. They are tools, not simulator code, so copying them is not an exception to the rule that v2 inherits no code. Once copied, v2 uses its own.

### What v2 must never rebuild

The new tree never contains any of these.

| Do not rebuild |
|---|
| Abandoned experiment B1 `min_bid_to_win`, its flag, emit, schema entries, pipeline handling and test literals |
| Abandoned experiments B2 and B3, the `explore_traffic` flag, branch and tombstones, and the v8 competition variant with its price multipliers and `ev_market` |
| Rival probes `rival_hidden` and `rival_user_corr`, and `n_rival_seg`, which never had a settings key |
| Draw-and-throw-away shims, the legacy rival settings fallback, presence-filtered column logic, and the streaming training fork |
| The region-tier table computed then dropped. The 3 tables v1 built and never read are not on this list. Open item O1 wired all 3 on 15 August 2026, so v2 builds them fresh |
| Never-read settings keys, the 12 calibration files the generator never reads at run time, v11 arm and diagram scripts, and stale analysis modules with a third seed convention |
| Package-root scratch files, tracked logs, the stale status file, superseded and live diagram generators, and the office document tooling |

One thing in v1 looks like clutter and is not. The separate random-number stream is what keeps the random jitter in our own bid independent of how valuable the impression is. v2 builds its own equivalent.


## 5. What is verified

*In brief.* 11 checks cover correctness, self-reproducibility, calibration and artifact retention, never agreement with v1's effect sizes. Generation and censoring are the deterministic stages, so those 2 write a content fingerprint and no other stage does. Training is not byte-identical twice, so it is held to a tolerance instead.

| Check | What it does | Stage | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| Startup checks V1 to V11 | run before any data is generated | 1, V3 in 2 | none, inside every command |
| Calibration file checksums | the 6 carried-over calibration CSVs are hashed at load and compared against the checksums recorded when they were copied, and a mismatch stops the run naming the file | 1 onward | none, at load |
| Import test | the single assertion in section 2, so no v2 import names v1's package | 1 onward | seconds |
| Per-law unit tests, independence gate | each law's drawn distribution matches the declared one, and the bid's exploration noise is independent of value | 2 | seconds |
| Calibration bands and direction checks | every calibrated quantity against its band in `validation.yaml`, and every direction check | 2 onward | none, inside every generation |
| ~~Golden fingerprints~~, chunk-size invariance | **The golden fingerprint was never built and is DROPPED, 22 Aug 2026.** No test compares generated output against a recorded hash, and gates 2 and 3 never mentioned one; only the fingerprint FUNCTION is tested, for writer, chunk-size and column-order independence and for row-order dependence. Dropped rather than built, because `generate.fingerprint` already hashes the generator settings AND the source bytes of the modules that draw the rows, so a refactor changes it, every dataset carries it, and `is_complete` refuses to mix generations. That is strictly better than a golden hash: per-dataset, automatic, and it fires at reuse rather than only when a test is run. What a golden hash would have added is a faster local signal, not a guarantee that is otherwise missing. Note it would NOT have caught the floor defect, which was wrong from stage 2 — a hash baselined then would have locked the bug in. Golden hashes catch changes, not initial wrongness. The chunk-size invariance test stays and is real | 2 and 3 | 2 generations for the invariance test |
| Dataset checksum manifest | one sha256 per campaign dataset, so any file that leaves this machine can be verified against the run that produced it. The golden fingerprint proves the code is stable, this proves a particular file is intact. Built at stage 7 as `t9v2/docs/gates/checksums.md` and `checksums.json` rather than the `t9v2/output/CHECKSUMS.txt` planned here, because `output/` is gitignored and a manifest that is not committed cannot be checked against later | 7 | one read of about 20 GB |
| Censoring leak checks | each view exposes exactly its declared observability, does not mutate the master, and never lets SSP-only columns reach C1 or C2 | 3 | one 100K censor, seconds |
| Winning-price leak test, ~~serving whitelist~~ | the leak tests were built: no row sees its own winning price through either encoder, and the SSP encoder reaches C3 and C4 only. **The serving whitelist was not built in v2 and is built in v2.2** — nothing checked a model's feature manifest against its view's visible columns, so nothing structurally prevented a latent, an estimand or the oracle being served. Closed at step 5 by one shared `BANNED_FEATURES` constant that the gate-4 condition and `tests/test_no_leak.py` both import rather than restate, checked against each FITTED model's feature list. The suite also force-adds `min_winning_price` to a C3 fit and asserts win AUC ≥ 0.999, so the exclusion is shown to be load-bearing rather than merely present | 4 | seconds |
| Training reproducibility | the same profile and seed trained twice, thread count fixed, which measures the run-to-run spread the 0.002 tolerance has to cover | 4 | a second 100K pass, about 25 s |
| **Artifact retention** | a seed counts as complete only when its folder holds ALL of: master parquet and manifest, `results.json`, one frozen bundle per view, one per-row eval file per view. A separate test asserts that no `unlink`, `rmtree` or `os.remove` in the source targets anything under `output/`, and that no delete flag exists to opt into. ADDED 21 Aug 2026 after `run_arm1.py` deleted the master it had just generated, destroying the parquets, models and per-row eval files behind the corrected 1M results now tagged `v2-corrected-1M`. The prior rule was doc-only and did not prevent it, so it moves into the completeness check the campaign already runs. The deeper gap is that `main` never WRITES bundles or per-row eval files at all, so this check and the persistence rebuild are one piece of work | 5 | none, inside `is_complete` |

~~Re-baselining happens only in the commit that caused it, logged in `t9v2/docs/GOLDEN_LOG.md`.~~ **Dropped 22 Aug 2026 with the golden fingerprint above.** `GOLDEN_LOG.md` was referenced twice in this document and never created, so nothing was ever logged in it. The design fingerprint in each dataset manifest is the record of which generator produced which data.

Solving the 6 constants is a stage 2 action, not a recurring check. (The count moved twice on 16 August 2026. It read 8; `ltv.lognormal_sigma` made it 9, because v2 had inherited v1's solved value while routing it `specified` and v1's provenance table records it as an autocal output; then the 3 archetype LTV means left it, because they were routed `auto-calibrated` while no solver had ever produced them. All 3 plus sigma aim at one scalar, so only sigma is identified. The named list with a target for each is `t9v2/config/calibrated.yaml`, in a `contract` block the solver writes against, and it now matches what the solver delivers.) It runs when a law changes, writes `calibrated.yaml` and costs roughly 10 minutes, v1's figure and unmeasured for v2. Re-solving cannot fail on its own, because the search is deterministic, so staleness is caught by the bands instead.

The reproducibility tolerance is 0.002 absolute on every AUC and 1 percent relative on CRPS, declared in `validation.yaml` as `repro_tolerance`, and a run outside it fails. Profit is not judged at 100K, so it is not in this test. The training manifest records the fingerprint chain, the settings hashes, the xgboost version and the thread count. A settings hash is a sha256 over the effective settings.

## 6. Phase 2 and Phase 3

*In brief.* Phase 2 and 3 get plug-in points, not implementations. **Of the four this section promised, one was built. The other three are outstanding and are the gap between v2 being a sound study and v2 being a platform.**

v2 was to build the plug-in points the later phases need, and nothing else. Prediction is single row and each head is saved as XGBoost native JSON plus its manifest. A bidder is one object, `bid(ev, pwin_curve, constraints) -> price`, where `pwin_curve` is the chance of winning at each candidate price. The oracle bidder, retained-truth scoring, and the estimand and latent columns are never served, which the serving whitelist enforces.

### What was actually built, checked against the code on 17 August 2026

| Plug-in point | State | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| **Prediction contract** | **BUILT** | `api.py` `Trained.score()` batch and `.predict()` single row; gate 4 checks they agree to 1e-9 |
| **Bidder protocol** | **NOT BUILT** | `api.py:74` `Trained.bid()` hardcodes argmax over the shared ladder. There is no `bid(ev, pwin_curve, constraints) -> price` interface a caller can implement and substitute, and `run_policies` names its 3 policies inline rather than resolving them through one |
| **Serving whitelist** | **NOT BUILT** | 0 references to `whitelist` anywhere in `src/`. Nothing checks a model's feature list against its view's visible columns, so the guarantee that latents, estimands and the oracle are never served rests on the feature builders being written correctly rather than on a check |
| **Model persistence** | **NOT BUILT** | no `save_model` or `load_model`. A `Trained` object exists only in the process that fitted it, so a model cannot be shipped, received, or re-scored later |

**Why this was missed.** Gate 7's conditions are tests green, stages 2 and 3 reproducing, the deferred list matching, and the checksum manifest. None of them asks whether the plug-in points this section promised exist, so all seven gates passed with three of four unbuilt. The deferred list was also verified honestly and did not catch it, because these three were never *on* the deferred list — they were promised as built.

**What each costs, and why they matter more than their size.**

| Piece | Work | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Bidder protocol | one abstract method, plus routing `run_policies` through it | phase 3's whole premise is a stranger benchmarking their own bidding algorithm against the oracle ceiling. Without it there is nowhere to plug one in |
| Serving whitelist | a set-intersection check between served features and the latent/estimand set, run at fit time | phase 3 hands the schema to someone who did not write the feature builders. The current guarantee is a convention, and a convention is exactly what a stranger will breach |
| Model persistence | XGBoost native JSON save/load plus the manifest already specified above | needed for phase 2 as well as 3: comparing methods across sessions means models that outlive the process that fitted them |

Together roughly half a day. **They should be built before v2 is offered for review as a platform**, as opposed to as a completed study — the study stands without them, and the phases do not.

Note the distinction that matters when reading the next paragraph: the 8 items below were **deferred by decision** and verified absent at gate 7. The 3 items above were **promised and not delivered**. They are different kinds of gap and should not be filed together.

8 things are deferred, each named and unimplemented. The `benchmarks/` folder. Deep models and serving infrastructure. The all-rows, won-rows and lost-rows scorecard. Diagrams generated from the settings file. The sequence dataset builder, history-based models and the schema-mapping layer. Bid shading, budget pacing, other auction formats and hyperparameter search. Method comparison, so v2 builds the XGBoost stack only. The provenance pass on the A3, A4 and A5 marginals.

### Added at stage 5, to be produced by the 10M campaign

**`ev_spearman`, the rank correlation of the chained ev against `ev_truth`.** v1 reports it as one of its four headline Tier-1 metrics (1M: C1 0.445, C2 0.552, MMP +0.0443 [+0.0240, +0.0646] 10/10). v2 previously had no equivalent: the per-head AUCs score the four heads separately, and `ev_ratio` mixes valuation with the win curve and the bid ladder, so nothing scored Tier 1 **as a whole**.

**Now implemented, and deliberately not backfilled** (Ken, 16 Aug 2026). It lives in `train/bidders.py:ev_bias`, is called once per view from `train/runner.py`, and lands in `results.json` under `views.<C>.ev` as `spearman` (all rows, the v1-comparable figure), `spearman_active` (`ev_truth > 0` only) and `n_active`. The same block carries `ratio`, which is v1's `ev_ratio` — mean predicted ev over mean true ev, its EV-bias diagnostic — under a name that cannot be confused with the value-capture `ev_ratio` in `economics`.

The existing 21 datasets are NOT re-scored, so they carry no `ev` block. The metric arrives with the 10M campaign, which is where the headline is reported; a mixed set where some seeds have it and some do not is the cost, and it is accepted rather than paid down, because training is the expense and time is short. The one exception already on disk is 100K seed 20250, re-trained as the smoke test, which gave `ratio` C1 0.562 to C2 0.963 against v1's 0.52 to 0.89 — the MMP selection-bias correction reproduced independently.

The rank correlation is written out rather than taken from scipy so the tie handling is explicit, and is verified equal to `scipy.stats.spearmanr` to machine precision on continuous, correlated, heavy-tie and ev-shaped inputs.

It is also v1's diagnostic for whether any learnable value signal exists at all. `docs/BN_Design_Investigation.md:14` records it moving 0.08 to 0.89 when the dependency edges were wired, with MMP profit going from minus $1,383 to plus $1,047 alongside it; :81 names edge #1's user-app pairing as the lever. A collapse in this number would mean the dependency layer had broken, and no other metric v2 carries would say so.

**Both cuts are reported, and the second is not redundant.** About 30 percent of rows are the inactive archetype at exactly zero, and a tie block that size takes the average rank of its whole run, so it can move the all-rows figure when nothing about the model has changed. The all-rows number is kept for comparability with v1; the active-only number is the one that says whether the model orders the rows a bidder would ever compete for.

## 6b. The substitution question, and why it is parked

*In brief.* Whether the constructed data can stand in for the proprietary integrated data that does
not exist publicly was examined on 24 August 2026 and **parked**. It is not answerable from this
build, and the reason is worth recording because it is a property of the calibration rather than an
oversight.

**A substitution claim has three steps and this build performs only the third.** To say the synthetic
data stands in for X, X must first be described, then the characteristics of X that matter for the
purpose must be named, and only then can the constructed data be shown to meet them. The build
calibrates and gates, which is step three applied to targets that were never assembled into a
statement of what X is.

**Every external anchor is a fitting target, not a test.** Of about 172 settings across `config/`,
122 are `inferred`, 26 `specified`, 7 `auto`, and only **17** are `quoted` against an outside source.
Each of those 17 was fitted to and then gated on. The clearest case is the win rate, whose source
reads "iPinYou 23.8 percent empirical rescaled; the same target validation.yaml gates on" — set to a
number, then checked against that number. `population_ctr` behaves the same way, solved to 0.035.
**No statistic in this study is held out.** The seven gates test internal consistency, the direction
sweeps test that the generator responds to its own parameters, and byte-identical reproduction tests
determinism. None compares the data to anything outside itself.

**What can be defended without it.** The ablation's internal validity does not depend on realism at
all. C1 and C2 are the same rows with different columns visible, so any difference between two views
is the data and nothing else. Realism decides whether a magnitude generalises to a real market; it has
no bearing on whether the comparison is sound. This is the stronger claim and it is the one to make.

**The one genuinely emergent quantity, and it was not noticed until now.** `population_ctr` is a
calibration target, but **no AUC appears anywhere in `config/`**. Predictive performance is therefore
emergent rather than fitted, and click AUC at 0.706 sits inside the range published CTR models report
on real data. That is the closest thing to a held-out check the study contains, it costs nothing to
state, and it is the only external comparison available today.

**What would answer it, if time allowed.** Describe X from public sources, which is possible even
though X cannot be obtained: OpenRTB 2.6 for the field inventory, iPinYou for what a DSP-side log
carries, MMP documentation for post-install measurement, mediation reports for supply-side reporting.
Then state the characteristics and check each. Eight were drafted and measured on 24 August:

| | Characteristic of X | Verdict on this build |
|---|---|---|
| X1 | Field coverage across the three layers | met, 56 columns, 31 visible to C1 and 38 to C4 |
| X2 | A gated funnel, no click meaning no install ever | met, enforced exactly in `gen/funnel.py` |
| X3 | Deep sparsity | met, click 3.49 percent, install 1.15, payers 0.040 |
| X4 | Heavy-tailed spend | met, the top tenth of payers take 57.6 percent of spend |
| X5 | Censoring of outcomes and of price | met, the C1 to C4 map is exactly this |
| X6 | Price formation against competitors | **partial**, rivals are drawn from a distribution and do not react |
| X7 | Value and price correlated | met weakly, rho 0.254 on logs, and lost rows carry higher true value than won |
| X8 | A join key linking the layers on one auction | **met but idealised**, the join is perfect and a real stack pays a matching tax |

X6 is the limitation AuctionNet levels at AdCraft and it applies here. X8 makes every layer-value
figure in this study an **upper bound**: a real integrated stack loses rows to attribution windows and
device-identifier loss, and none of that is modelled. Both belong in the limitations section whether
or not the substitution question is ever answered.

## 7. Change log

*In brief.* What this revision of the plan changed, and what the build records as it runs.

Changes in this revision.

1. v2 inherits no code from v1. `api.py`, the README and the checksum script are written fresh, and the v1 module map is replaced by v2's own layout.
2. `docs/KDD_Terminology.md` joins the input pack and binds v2's names. `visibility` becomes `observability`, `view(master, condition)` becomes `censor(master, view)`, and `hist_clearing` becomes `hist_winning_price`. The `clearing_price` column becomes `winning_price`, decided at open item O10, with the count still 55.
3. The design sheet is gone. Its open items moved into the specification, beside the design they change. Part C stops being a signed table and becomes a generated conformance check.
4. The negative control is dropped. v1 established that the rival-pool design produces the C3 minus C1 gap, and re-testing it in v2 bought only 16 percent headroom against its own bound. The leak tests at stages 3 and 4 stay.
5. Overpay is not a v2 metric. 8 figures are scored, the 4 AUCs, the spend CRPS, profit with `ev_ratio`, and ECE and MCE per head per view, measured and never fitted (open item O7). Tier 2 has one head, the win classifier; the AFT head is not rebuilt, so no price metric is scored.
10. A failed direction check no longer means re-running a seed, which is impossible on deterministic generation. The seed list is fixed, and a lone failure is read at the larger scales instead. The Risks section is deleted, since every row in it restated a gate or a guard stated earlier.
11. v2 copies no value from v1's settings files unattributed. Stage 1 builds the 7 files from the documents and `tools/report_holes.py` reports the holes, the unsourced values and the undeclared keys. The gate-1 provenance sweep of 15 August closed 24 of the 25; the last, `spend_model.scale`, is open item O12 and is decided at stage 4.
9. v2's folder and package are renamed from `t9sim_v2` and `t9sim2` to `t9v2`, so no v2 name contains v1's `t9sim` as a substring. Free to do now, since no code exists yet.
8. The switched-off variants are dropped. The 6 dependencies are always wired, every node carries one law, and v1's 8 variant-only rows and its all-OFF byte-identity gate do not carry over. Open item O11.
7. The data campaign stops being its own section and moves inside section 3, under the stages table, because it described stages 5 and 6 a second time. Sections 5 to 10 renumber down to 4 to 9.
6. Sections 5 and 7 are merged into one section 5 about v1, holding what is protected and what carries over. Section 6 keeps its number and the 4 sections after it drop by 1.

What the build records as it runs.
